News.title: Britain will go bankrupt under Burnham, warns Kemi Badenoch as she accuses PM of saying YES to every spending demand
News.content:
BRITAIN will go bankrupt under Andy Burnham’s leadership because he refuses to say no to colleagues asking for more funds, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch claimed yesterday.

She insisted that his first statement to the Commons as PM on Tuesday made his problem clear — despite turmoil on the money markets over his grip on public finances.



Probed on whether he will bankrupt the country, she said: “If you listen to his statement, I think the answer is ‘probably’, because he had so many requests for government spending, so many requests for taxpayers’ money.

“He didn’t say no to anything.



“If someone doesn’t know how to say no, then they will run out of money.

“The problem with socialism is they always run out of other people’s money, not their own.”



Meanwhile, senior Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry said she expected taxes to rise at next month’s Budget.

She pointed to “huge strains” on the economy as Chancellor John Healey grapples with inflation, the Iran War and an estimated £14billion blow to finances owing to increases in the Government’s borrowing costs.

Economists believe an estimated £14billion has been wiped away from the Government’s financial cushion due to the hikes in borrowing costs.

Lord O’Neill, an ally of the PM, says the bond markets would welcome the Government tackling the “sacred cows” such as the triple lock or welfare costs to get on top of the public finances.

News.title: Doctors warned over second jobs after ‘exhausted’ consultant found dead in hospital staff room following night shift
News.content:
TRAGIC DEATH Doctors warned over second jobs after ‘exhausted’ consultant found dead in hospital staff room following night shift

DOCTORS have been warned about the dangers of taking second jobs after an “exhausted” consultant was found dead in a hospital staff room.

Naeem Ahmed, 50, was discovered slumped in a chair at Poole Hospital in Dorset after finishing his ninth 13-hour night shift in a row.



The consultant in anaesthesia and pain medicine was pronounced dead at the scene on June 21 last year.

A post-mortem examination found traces of alcohol and the synthetic opioid fentanyl in his blood.



An inquest heard Dr Ahmed had just completed his ninth 13-hour night shift in a row and he had also been working extra hours during the day for a private provider.

Senior coroner Rachael Griffin has now issued a warning over the risks of doctors working across different employers.

She said current NHS systems do not take into account the total workload of doctors who have jobs with more than one provider.

The coroner warned this could result in “continuous periods of working without rest”.

She said that could put the lives of both patients and doctors at risk.

The inquest heard Dr Ahmed, a father of three who was born in Pakistan, had started drinking and taking fentanyl as a “mental crutch to help calm his mind”.



His wife Laura, a paediatric doctor who had been married to him for 23 years, also raised concerns about the impact of sleep deprivation.

She described her husband as “kind and patient” and a “good dad who took his responsibilities to provide for his children very seriously”.

Mrs Ahmed said he had been taking the opioid painkiller tramadol for lower back pain since 2018.

She believed he continued taking it even after his back problems had improved.

Dr Ahmed died while working the ninth shift in a run of 11 night shifts for University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust.



The run began on June 12, 2025.

Coroner Griffin said Dr Ahmed had carried out clinical work for more than one provider on the same day on several occasions.

On one occasion, he worked during the day for an external provider before starting a resident overnight shift for the NHS trust later that day.

She said the systems used for job planning, rostering and secondary employment operated independently.

They were “not designed to provide an integrated view” of a doctor’s workload across different employers.



The coroner said there was no legal requirement for doctors to tell NHS trusts about their private work patterns, or private providers about their NHS work.

She warned that this could allow doctors to work continuously without adequate rest.

Griffin said the trust had taken steps to address the issue, but she remained concerned the same problem could exist at other trusts across England and Wales.

She said this could lead to fatigue and potentially “fatal outcomes” for patients and doctors.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The coroner has sent her report to the health minister and the chief executive of NHS England so similar action can be considered elsewhere.



She recorded Dr Ahmed’s death as one of misadventure.

News.title: Reality TV stars Gabby Allen and Emily Miller join calls for Freeview switch-off to be pushed back
News.content:
FIGHT FOR FREEVIEW Reality TV stars Gabby Allen and Emily Miller join calls for Freeview switch-off to be pushed back

REALITY TV stars tonight joined demands for the Freeview switch-off to be pushed back into the 2040s.

They are calling on Andy Burnham to help millions of people who fear the terrestrial platform could be switched off in 2034.



Gabby Allen, a star of ITV’s Love Island and Celebrity Big Brother, said: “Millions of households still rely on these services to stay connected.

“For many people there isn’t a straightforward alternative because of where they live, what they can afford or the technology they’re able to use.”



Too Hot to Handle star Emily Miller added: “I really don’t think millions of people, including the older generation and people who simply can’t afford other means of staying connected, should lose access to it.”

The Sun’s Save Our Sets campaign is demanding free TV is protected rather than forcing viewers into paying for internet-based services.



Ministers are consulting on proposals to end traditional terrestrial television broadcasts and deliver TV over the internet instead, with ministers considering a switch-off from 2034 or delaying it until 2044.

Prime Minister Burnham told MPs this week he was “concerned” about the plans and vowed to “have a proper look at it”.

He added: “I know some of my constituents in Makerfield rely on Freeview. There is perhaps an opportunity to look at this as part of the BBC Charter renewal process.

“I recognise it’s a genuine issue…I know it will be of concern to constituents and let me have a proper look at it.”



Polling shows four in five people would be angry if free-to-air TV was switched off in 2034. Nearly seven in 10 said any government doing so would be out of touch with ordinary people.

A Save Free TV spokesman said: “The Prime Minister is right to be worried, and the whole country agrees with him.

“Younger people also want free TV protected, because they know their parents and grandparents depend on it. It’s time to rule out a 2034 switch off for good and keep it running to 2044 at the least”

News.title: Laughing gas offences soar despite drug being banned, shock figures show
News.content:
LAUGHING gas offences have soared despite the drug being banned, Home Office figures show.

They also reveal that seven in ten of those caught go unpunished.



Police in England and Wales recorded at least 5,780 offences of possessing nitrous oxide in the year to March 2026.

It is a rise of 76 per cent on 2025 — the first full year of the ban on the Class C drug, often inhaled from balloons.



Possession of the gas to get high can carry up to two years in jail.

But 70 per cent of resolved cases to the end of March this year ended with an informal community resolution with no criminal record.

Just 12 per cent ended with the offender being charged.

Despite the figures, the Government claimed reported use of the gas is at its “lowest level since records began”.

Zaheen Ahmed, Head of Therapy at addiction treatment experts The UKAT Group said: “Nitrous oxide addiction is becoming increasingly prevalent.

“Even as a residential rehab provider – which is the vast majority of people’s last resort – we’re seeing a sharp rise in calls for help and admissions relating to the drug.



“There are still widespread assumptions that nitrous oxide isn’t addictive, doesn’t carry serious health risks, or comes without criminal consequences.

“All three assumptions are wrong.

“Nitrous oxide is no laughing matter, and we’re seeing it ruin lives in the same way other substances do.”

News.title: Two cops injured after ‘stolen car crashes into marked police vehicle during chase’ – as teen, 16, arrested
News.content:
SMASH HORROR Two cops injured after ‘stolen car crashes into marked police vehicle during chase’ – as teen, 16, arrested

A 16-YEAR-OLD has been arrested after allegedly smashing into a police car during a chase – hospitalising two officers.

The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, has been charged with several offences following the incident in Grimsby, Lincolnshire, yesterday.

Humberside Police were scrambled to the scene on Byron Grove after receiving reports of a car being stolen at around 1pm.

Officers pursued the motor before the chase came to an end when the car allegedly ploughed into a marked police vehicle.





Two officers were injured in the chase and taken to hospital for treatment.

The teen was arrested and has since been charged with several offences including dangerous driving, possession of a class C drug, theft and two counts of driving without a licence.

He has also been charged with two counts of driving without insurance, making off without payment, taking a motor vehicle, possession of a class B drug, aggravated vehicle taking and driving a vehicle without the owner’s consent.

He has been remanded into secure accommodation to appear in court at a later date.



Humberside Police said: “At around 1pm officers received reports of a car being stolen resulting in a pursuit.

“The car then allegedly collided with a marked police vehicle, resulting in both vehicles coming to a stop and two officers being taken to hospital to receive treatment to injuries.”

News.title: Thrill seekers spend FOUR hours dangling 100ft in air after pendulum ride malfunctions at fairground
News.content:
A GROUP of thrill seekers spent four hours suspended 100ft in the air after their fairground ride malfunctioned.

The terrifying ordeal unfolded when the “Gigant” pendulum ride, which can reach 164ft in height, came to a complete standstill.



The ride suffered an unexpected technical failure shortly after 11pm on Friday.

It left seven people suspended between 98ft above the ground on the penultimate night of the 2026 Almería Fair in Spain.



Local cops rushed to the scene after receiving reports of the stranded riders before cordoning off the area.

Fears for their safety grew worse when firefighters failed to reach them during initial rescue attempts.

But by 1.30am, emergency teams managed to reach the trapped group.

Firefighters, from Almería and Poniente, carefully rescued all seven thrill seekers one by one during the operation.



Rescue efforts were complicated by the fact that the ride’s passenger gondola could rotate.

This meant that removing one person would change the distribution of weight – potentially affecting the distribution of weight on the structure.

The rescue was therefore carried out gradually.



Emergency services worked from different points around the gondola to control its movements and maintain safe conditions at all times.

Eventually, by 3am, the last trapped passenger reached the ground – wrapping up the group’s four hellish hours of torment.

But those on the ride were not the only people affected by the malfunction.

Concertgoers watching Mestiza perform at the fairground’s Concert Venue had their gig cancelled so firefighters could carry out the rescue operation without disruption.

Authorities said: “Complicated and delicate operation. Congratulations to our colleagues on the work carried out.



“Thanks to Bomberos del Poniente for their assistance.”

News.title: What did love-in between Burnham and Macron ACTUALLY achieve? Don’t expect migrant crossings to stop for a start
News.content:
French folly

WHAT did yesterday’s love-in between Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron actually achieve?

For a start, don’t expect the small boats to stop any time soon.



It’s still hugely in France’s interest to let migrants set sail and wait for British border forces to rescue them – especially as we pay £1billion for the privilege.

Burnham’s welcoming of a measly 45 extra officers to patrol hundreds of miles of northern French coastline shows the Government is still pathetically grateful for minimum French support.



Yesterday, he couldn’t help gushing over France’s role in another terrible idea: helping him achieve closer ties to the EU. Sir Keir Starmer was conned by Macron into huge giveaways as part of his notorious “reset”.

That included meekly taking rules and standards on food and energy and agreeing to a “youth mobility” scheme for EU workers under 30.



After the summit it seems we must now prepare for further betrayals of Brexit by Burnham.

But if he thinks binding Britain to the EU is the answer, the PM must be even more confused about economic reality than we thought.

Even Britain’s flat-lining economy has outperformed France, Germany and other European nations since Brexit.

Precious few “postcodes” across the EU have seen any growth.



How would further cosying up to Brussels help Burnham deliver it here?

Indefensible

HOW much more damage can Labour’s dithering over defence spending inflict?

Never mind actually fighting the Russians in a real war.

As we reveal today, Army top brass are now so cash-strapped they can’t even afford for soldiers to PRACTISE.

Forcing the axe of major war games with immediate effect is unprecedented.



It is a terrifying example of the decline forced on our military by useless politicians who care more about delivering the next welfare cheque than protecting the country from Vladimir Putin.

Last night, Argentinian president Javier Milei used a nationwide TV address to tell his people they have a “sacred right” to the Falkland Islands.

What chance would Britain have of defending them now?

Loss of Power

THE grim news that Paddy Power could shut 100 high street shops is proof of the insanity of this Government’s war on fun.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Around 400 jobs are now at risk, adding to those suffered in closures already announced by William Hill and Betfred.



Labour’s senseless taxes and intrusive affordability checks are sending regulated firms to the wall while driving punters into the arms of online black market gangs.

News.title: I’ll declare a national emergency on my first day as PM & sack any minister who fails to deliver, Nigel Farage will vow
News.content:
REFORM UK leader Nigel Farage will today pledge to declare a “national emergency” on his first day as PM.

He will also vow to sack any minister who fails to deliver.



In his conference speech, Mr Farage plans to tell party activists that MPs should “sit day and night” to crash through urgent laws and fight civil service resistance.

He aims to use the speech as a reset following Reform’s dip in the polls.



Mr Farage has been dogged by questions about an undeclared £5million gift and is facing a Commons probe.

The Brexiteer will use his opening address to prove he is still focused on becoming PM and has a plan for No10.

He will say: “Within days of winning the general election, we will introduce dozens of bills and force Parliament to sit all through summer for seven days a week to pass them.

“Britain is in serious trouble. We don’t have time to wait around to fix it”.

Key issues for the would-be PM are the illegal migration crisis and the cost of living.

He would compel Parliament to sit round-the-clock and even through the summer holidays should he win power.



Anticipating pushback from the Whitehall machine, he will say: “If the Lords, judiciary or civil service get in our way they will discover just how determined we are” and will commit to doing “anything and everything to make the first 100 days work”.

And he will warn any ministers who fail to get on top of their brief have “no place in my cabinet”.

Reform is tied at 23 per cent with Andy Burnham’s Labour after surrendering their 15-month lead, according to a “poll of polls”.

One recent survey even had Mr Farage dipping below Kemi Badenoch’s Tory party.

But despite the setbacks, he will insist the party was “much stronger than we were last year” and add: “I believe that Reform can win it.”



Mr Farage won the Clacton by-election he himself triggered to win the judgement of his constituents over the £5million gift scandal.

He could be forced to fight another contest should he be sanctioned by Parliament’s Standards Commissioner.

News.title: Pig kidney transplant let man live without needing dialysis for nine months in world-first
News.content:
A man has had a pig kidney successfully transplanted into him for nine months while he awaited a human kidney.

Doctors are hailing the procedure as a world-first as a “bridge” organ as millions around the world are on transplant waiting lists to get human organs.

Tim Andrews, who had end-stage kidney disease, was 66 when he received the genetically modified pig kidney in the US last year. He then lived successfully with the genetically edited organ for 271 days without dialysis before getting a donor human kidney.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham hospitals groups said this is the longest dialysis-free survival following a pig kidney transplant and the first transition from pig to human kidney transplantation.

‌



View 7 Images Tim before surgeons operated on him (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

View 7 Images Tim Andrews said the pig kidney gave him a life (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

NHS transplant landmark sees turbo charged lungs ‘breathe’ outside of body READ MORE :

New NHS technique means hundreds of organs will be saved for lifesaving transplants READ MORE :

Tim has told a CNN documentary that the pig kidney transplant was a "miracle", and added: "I was alive and I hadn't been in a long time."

Tim had kidney failure caused by type 2 diabetes and had been living on dialysis before receiving the pig kidney from a Yucatan miniature pig. He said he was now able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog Cupcake. Details of the breakthrough in xenotransplantation - which means animal-to-human - are published in the Lancet medical journal.

‌



View 7 Images The kidney from a Yucatan miniature pig (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

Lead author Dr Leonardo Riella said: "The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation. We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don't have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.

"Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap - initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right."

It comes as the UK organ donor waiting list is at a record high after a post-pandemic downturn in families approving transplants in deceased relatives.

‌



View 7 Images The kidney being transplanted by the team of surgeons (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

Scientists used gene editing to genetically engineer the organ to be compatible with his human immune system - so the body would not recognise it as from another species and reject it.

After six months scientists identified damage in the kidney's blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the pig kidney was removed and replaced by a kidney from a dead human donor.

The milestone follows the case of American Rick Slayman who was the first person to receive a genetically modified pig kidney at Massachusetts General Hospital in 2024.

‌



Medics hailed the operation as a success but the 62-year-old died two months later. The Massachusetts hospital said at the time there was no indication his death was a result of the transplant.

View 7 Images Tim recovering after his op (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

Mr Andrews’ case gives fresh hope that pig organs could one day be safe enough to become part of the answer to the global shortage in organs for transplant. Before then scientists say they could be used as a bridge before a human organ comes available.

Dr Rommel Ravanan, chief medical officer for NHS Blood and Transplant in the UK, said: "Advances in genetics technology enable teams to `knock out' some of the pig genes, so the human body is less able to recognise [that] the organ was different. Pigs are chosen for several reasons, including that their organ size and anatomy is similar to that of a human.”

‌



View 7 Images Tim after the op went well (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

Dr Riella said: "The patients are the true pioneers here. By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early-stage studies, they are advancing the science.”

The Department of Health and Social Care has now set up an advisory group to help advise ministers on the ethics around pig transplants.

Dr Ravanan added: "It's important to recognise that, even if shown to be effective, there is still a very long way to go before these kinds of transplants could become an everyday reality.

‌



View 7 Images Tim in an emotional embrace with his wife just before leaving the hospital (Image: Kate Flock/Massachusetts General Hospital/PA Wire)

"With the transplant waiting list at an all-time high, and people dying on the transplant waiting list every day, there is an urgent need for more people to support organ donation by joining the NHS Organ Donor Register and talking to their family about their wish to be an organ donor."

To find out more and to register an organ donation decision call 0300 123 23, visit organdonation.nhs.uk or use the NHS app.

News.title: One dead after Tesla strikes pedestrians in car park as four suffer injuries
News.content:
One dead after Tesla strikes pedestrians in car park as four suffer injuries

A car has crashed into pedestrians in a grocery store car park leaving one dead and four hospitalised

View 2 Images Car crash kills one and leaves four injured (Image: FOX LOCAL LA)

One person has been killed after being struck by a car in a grocery store car park.

‌



The incident took place in a car park of a Trader Joe's in Los Angeles on Thursday afternoon.

‌



Officials said the Tesla crashed into a security stand, killing one and injuring at least four others.

‌



View 2 Images The incident took place near busy Trader Joe's (Image: FOX LOCAL LA)

The store is based on Third Street and Fairfax Avenue.

‌



Los Angeles Fire Department crews responded to the crash near the Trader Joe’s in the Beverly Grove area around 1.20 pm, with police also attending the scene.

The LAFD confirmed that one person was pronounced dead at the scene as four others were treated by emergency services.

They have been rushed to hospital.

Article continues below

The driver reportedly lost control of her vehicle, causing her to hit a parked car and the pedestrians before smashing into the security stand, NBC reports.

The driver has been described as an 80-year-old woman, who has also been hospitalised.

This is a breaking news story, more to follow.

News.title: Brits warned to stock up on days of supplies as UN issues 'supersize' El Nino warning
News.content:
Brits warned to stock up on days of supplies as UN issues 'supersize' El Nino warning

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle warned Brits needed to be better prepared in the face of environmental emergencies that could hit with the 'largest' El Nino

View 4 Images Brits have been told to prepare for extreme weather (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A government minister has warned Brits to "store of a bit of food" and prepare for possible national emergencies as the UN warns of an incoming "supersized" El Nino.

‌



The public was urged to have a supply of water and food that would last a few days in the event of a climate disaster. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the high chance the UK could experience a rough winter after battling five heatwaves this summer alone. The minister added that people are about to experience "probably the largest El Nino that has ever been seen" and warned "we need to take it seriously".

‌



This comes after UN head António Guterres said the planet was in "uncharted waters" and warned: "El Nino is being supersized before our eyes."

‌



UK weather maps show 3C chill as Brits face shock cold snap in weeks READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Thursday with 33 counties at risk READ MORE :

View 4 Images Angela Eagle said Brits need to be better prepared for potential climate-related emergencies (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The Environment Secretary's strong urged Brits to prepare for potential environmental emergencies that could hit the UK amid the brewing weather phenomena.

Dame Eagle, speaking to the the Guardian, said: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Nino that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country. It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

‌



"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

View 4 Images UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres issued a warning over the impact of El Nino (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Dame Eagle, speaking from Havant Thicket - set to be the UK's first new reservoir since 1992, added that the UK needed to do its "own adaptations" in the face of a changing climate.

‌



El Nino is declared when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise are 0.5C or more above average. This weather pattern, which happens around every 2-7 years, impacts global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.

Wind that usually blows across the east to the west of the Pacific Ocean can weaken or stop, which allows warm water to move east. This heat can then be released from the ocean and into the atmosphere, leading a temperature rise of 0.5C or more.

View 4 Images Fires have been burning in parts of Indonesia since mid-July (Image: Ahmad Fauzi Herdiansyah/JNA via ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

‌



The heat from El Nino has already impacted regions with the monsoon in Indian seeing less rain than average this year and fires burning in parts of Indonesia since mid-July.

The brewing El Nino is expected to last into 2027 and with the impact of human-induced climate change next year could "very likely" be the hottest on record, the Met Office previously said.

UN Secretary General Guterres called for urgent action to be taken, saying: "El Nino is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. The world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”

Article continues below

Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, described this year's El Nino as "an unprecedented event". He said: "I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts... if the forecast is accurate, and other forecast systems show similar extreme values, then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Nino and its worldwide climate influences."

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after two crashes on M5 motorway near Bristol
News.content:
Attempted murder arrest after two crashes on M5 motorway near Bristol

Police have arrested a man on suspicion of attempted murder following two collisions at the meeting point of the M4 and M5 motorways near Bristol

View Image The collisions sparked major traffic on two motorways (Image: Bristol Live)

A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after two collisions on a busy motorway interchange.

‌



Avon and Somerset Police were called to the meeting point of the M4 and M5 motorways at the Almondsbury Interchange, near Bristol, at around 9pm on Wednesday.

‌



It followed a report that a car had collided with the central reservation on the M5 northbound, before the driver got out of his vehicle and there was a second crash involving two vehicles on the M4.

‌



National Highways announced a closure of the motorway and said at the time that traffic could not join the M4 westbound from either direction. The collisions happened at junction 20 of the M5 and junction 15 at the Almondsbury Interchange.

Witnesses told how drivers had started exiting their vehicles on the motorway while the traffic was at a standstill and emergency services got to work.

Avon and Somerset Police have now provided more details of the events on Wednesday night and the circumstances surrounding the road closure, reports Bristol Live.

‌



A man has since been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder, and on suspicion of being unfit to drive through drink or drugs. He remains in hospital with "potentially life changing" injuries, police said.

A spokesperson said: "We were called at just after 9pm yesterday on Wednesday 2 September to the Almondsbury interchange on the M5 northbound and M4 westbound following reports of a collision.

"The initial report was of a car which had collided with the central reservation of the carriageway. The driver of the car then got out of his vehicle and was involved in a further collision involving two other vehicles travelling on the M4 carriageway.

‌



"The driver and passenger of the initial vehicle were taken to hospital, where the passenger has since been discharged.

"The driver, who has been arrested and remains under police supervision in hospital, is not thought to have life-threatening injuries but are potentially life changing.

"The drivers of the other cars involved are aiding us with our enquiries and are being treated as witnesses. Both carriageways were closed while emergency services attended but reopened at 10.30pm yesterday.

Article continues below

"If you have any information, or witnessed the collision or moments which followed, please call us on 101 and quote reference 5226252893."

News.title: Met Office forecasts temperatures to drop within days across 57 areas of UK - full list
News.content:
Met Office forecasts temperatures to drop within days across 57 areas of UK - full list

Temperatures are set to be below the average for this time of year across much of the UK next week

View 2 Images Temperatures are set to drop to below average in the second week of September (Image: Bristol Post)

Large parts of the UK are set for a dramatic change in temperatures as forecasts predict colder than average temperatures next week. Although meteorological autumn got underway from September 1, the coming weekend is expected to be warm with temperatures in the high 20s on Sunday.

‌



However, the Met Office is warning temperatures will drop back after the brief spell of warm weather. September 7 to 14 looks cooler than average, particularly across northern areas.

‌



In the update on the Met Office Youtube channel meteorologist Annie Shuttleworth said: “Temperatures are set to climb to the high 20s, but it’s pretty much a one-day only affair.”

‌



The warmer air isn’t expected to stick around, with conditions turning cooler again as low pressure pushes in. The forecaster explained: “It turns cooler again when we get more of a low pressure push in from the north.

View 2 Images Weather maps show large parts of the UK turning blue forecasting 'below average temperatures' from Sept 7 to 14 2026 (Image: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF))

The meteorologist said: “After an anomalous warm day on Sunday, next week actually looks cooler than average across many northern areas and pretty close to average for early September across southern areas.”

‌



She added that the UK is in for a 'bumpy run' of conditions, with temperatures swinging as weather fronts move through: “It’s going to be quite changeable temperature-wise throughout the next 10 days.”

Before the temperatures change, northern parts of the UK are set for a windy weekend, which could carry on into the start of next week. The strongest winds look most likely across northern and northwestern areas at times.

The Met Office forecaster said: “We could see gusts of around 40 mph across some northern areas on Friday afternoon.”

‌



Looking ahead to Sunday, she added there is “the potential for quite a breezy day”, with model guidance showing “some inland gusts of around 40 miles per hour” across parts of northern England, southern Scotland and northwestern Scotland.

News.title: FIFA accuse UEFA of launching 'smear campaign' against Gianni Infantino
News.content:
FIFA accuse UEFA of launching 'smear campaign' against Gianni Infantino

FIFA and UEFA's bitter public spat has taken another turn with the latter accused of launching a 'smear campaign' against Gianni Infantino following his plot to sell World Cup shares

View 2 Images Aleksandr Ceferin and Gianni Infantino do not see eye to eye (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

UEFA has been accused of running a "smear campaign" against Gianni Infantino by FIFA following the former's attempt to launch legal action over a failed plot to sell shares in the World Cup.

‌



Infantino was heavily criticised after unveiling a scheme to sell off shares in future FIFA tournaments to private investors, with UEFA's nations even threatening to boycott World Cups if the proposals were put into action.

‌



The 56-year-old eventually rowed back on the proposals but has been subjected to calls for his resignation, while it emerged last week that UEFA are preparing a criminal file against Infantino.

‌



They filed legal papers in the United States requesting the release of evidence and documents from FIFA. But they have responded with court filings of their own in which they accused UEFA of "a smear campaign against it and its leadership".

The governing body also claims that UEFA's argument suffers from "legal deficiencies". According to BBC Sport, the filings say: "UEFA seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that UEFA admittedly lacks the authority to initiate. Despite that threshold problem, UEFA asks this court to authorise sweeping discovery about the FFE."

‌



FIFA went on to stress that it had "made clear" the creation of FFE (Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme) was "only a proposal" and would not have proceeded without overwhelming support.

"Rather than participate in that democratic process, Uefa issued a press release - the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership," FIFA wrote.

In their court filing, UEFA described the creation of FFE as "a vehicle for Infantino and a small circle to acquire a permanent stake and otherwise profit from Fifa’s most valuable assets."

‌



View 2 Images Infantino's position has come under scrutiny in recent weeks (Image: Zac Goodwin/PA Wire)

The fallout of the proposals have left the two governing bodies at war, although UEFA has now dropped the threat of its nations boycotting future World Cup tournaments.

UEFA are also pushing for Joshua Kushner, a venture capitalist and the son-in-law of Donald Trump who was set to be the lead investor in FFE, for a testimony.

Article continues below

Kushner apologised for the abandoned venture on Sunday, saying: "While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to… had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved."

News.title: Berlin airport evacuated over 'security issue' - emergency services rush to scene
News.content:
Berlin airport evacuated over 'security issue' - emergency services rush to scene

Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport was evacuated after a woman walked to a service point and claimed to be carrying a dangerous substance, police said

View Image Berlin Brandenburg Airport (file image) (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Police swarmed Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) and ordered passengers to leave after a woman told security staff she was carrying a dangerous substance.

‌



Officers said the woman had walked to a service point inside the airport on Thursday evening and claimed to be carrying the substance, sparking concern amongst travellers.

‌



Experts are now investigating whether the woman was actually carrying any hazardous materials, Bild reports. According to the publication, the suspect did not make any threats.

‌



A police spokesman told Germany's DPA news agency that "a potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out."

Emergency personnel in protective suits were pictured outside the terminal this evening.

‌



The airport confirmed that the public area of Terminal 1 was evacuated "because of the suspicion of a dangerous substance."

A spokesman said the federal police issued a dangerous item alert at around 5:45pm, leading to the "public area of Terminal 1 being cleared."

Planes already preparing to depart were able to take off as normal, while incoming arrivals were also able to land.

Article continues below

Passenger processing was being "relocated to Terminal 2," the airport added. "The degree to which this could lead to delays or cancellations is not yet foreseeable."

News.title: Betting giant Paddy Power to shut up to 100 shops with 400 jobs at risk
News.content:
Betting giant Paddy Power to shut up to 100 shops with 400 jobs at risk

Paddy Power operate a total of 506 betting stores in Ireland and the UK right now with the proposed closures mean around one fifth of outlets could close

View 2 Images Up to 100 shops across the UK and Ireland could close (Image: Getty Images)

Up to 100 Paddy Power betting shops could be set to close before the end of the year, putting around 400 jobs at risk, owners Flutter Entertainment have announced.

‌



Those 100 stores would total around one-fifth of Paddy Power's entire Ireland and UK retail estate.

‌



Flutter blamed rising energy and rates costs, as well as the government's remote gaming duty rise have all taken a toll.

‌



“We are incredibly proud of our high street estate, and it remains a key part of our business in communities across the UK and Ireland. Unfortunately, we have had to take the extremely difficult decision to conduct this review," a spokesperson for Flutter UK and Ireland said.

"The high street trading environment has been challenging for a number of years given rising costs, fierce competition, economic uncertainty and the shift to online but we also face a material impact from the higher gambling taxes announced in last year’s UK budget.

"Our immediate priority at this time is to support those colleagues affected by this announcement."

‌



View 2 Images A punter places a bet in a bookmakers (Image: Getty)

Paddy Power owner Flutter posted tough Q2 trading results, with a $37m profit swinging to a $296m loss year-on-year for the New York Stock Exchange listed company, the Irish Mirror reports.

Flutter, who also own Sky Bet and Betfair, say that “impacted colleagues will be offered redeployment opportunities where possible”.

Article continues below

Paddy Power operate a total of 506 betting stores in Ireland and the UK right now

The Irish gambling company founded in 1988. Its product offering includes sports betting, online casino, online poker, and online bingo. Business operations are led from its headquarters in Dublin, alongside a satellite office in Malta.

Back in July, Betfred announced plans to close 132 stores, while William Hill owner Evoke are set to shut 270 of its betting shops.

News.title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
News.content:
Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of Â£500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.

Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".

The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.

Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.

Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor â his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come as soon as mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups successfully argued that consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will provide gas to supply up to 6% of the UK's demand at peak production, but environmental groups say it will only supply 2%.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and these updated estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Transplanted pig kidney works in US man's body for record 271 days
News.content:
A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days â the longest on record, say US doctors.

Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.

The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.

But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.

Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation â using organs from other species â due to shortages of organs for transplants.

In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.

Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.

"I had a little bit of a shortage of timeâ¦ it becomes very depressing," he said.

But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".

"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

News.title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
News.content:
The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.

It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.

But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.

The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.

A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales.

It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apache helicopters.

This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year.

Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army â such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.

The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis.

Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.

Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.

An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness.

"We are also investing Â£2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."

On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030.

The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."

The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces.

Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.

The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

News.title: Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support
News.content:
Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.

"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'

Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.

He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get â most of those countries get â a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".

Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

News.title: Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equality
News.content:
Gloria Steinem spent more than 60 years as one of the most prominent voices in the fight for women's rights.

She launched herself into the mainstream in the 1960s with an expose of New York City's Playboy Club, documenting the harsh conditions she faced working undercover as a Playboy Bunny.

A powerful and outspoken campaigner at a time of routine discrimination, Steinem faced sexist criticism and harassment from men throughout her long career.

Her lifelong battle saw many victories, including the US Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v Wade decision that guaranteed a woman's right to an abortion.

It also saw setbacks, like that same decision being overturned in 2022.

The feminist icon died on Wednesday at the age of 92, her foundation said in a statement. She never retired.

News.title: AI tools that take notes for GPs could miss vital information, study suggests
News.content:
The report concluded AI scribes can help with administrative work but more research needs to be done to understand how they work in specific healthcare settings and how their design supports both patients and clinicians.

It comes months after the BBC heard from doctors in the West Midlands, who said their workload had been significantly cut by using the transcription tool Heidi.

At one clinic in Dudley, the tool was credited with reducing a backlog of posting patient letters from six months to 14 days.

One of the key findings by the University of Edinburgh was that although AI tools can help capture what patients say, they can sometimes miss important aspects of consultations - such as facial expressions, gestures and emotional state.

The report said AI summaries tend to prioritise clinical information, which can come at the expense of the patients' stories and experiences of their illness.

It was also found that patients may be hesitant to reveal sensitive information - such as substance abuse, domestic abuse or mental health struggles - when they know the consultation is being recorded and processed by AI.

Researchers also highlighted that manual notetaking serves important functions for clinicians in their reasoning and reflection on what the patient has said.

Their report said using AI scribes could result in "cognitive offloading" for clinicians - which means the tools take on some of their mental effort.

This can have benefits, the report said, as clinicians can spent their efforts having more meaningful conversations with patients or concentrating on complex tasks.

However, it also said the tools can reduce memory recall and skill development and highlighted instances where clinicians do not recognise their own notes or remember the patient the next time they see them.

News.title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authority, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"As with any significant gathering, we have plans in place to ensure public safety and security, which is line with our usual process."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil, for one of the young men who died, last week was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

A total of 27 people have been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

News.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
News.content:
Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and Â£45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost Â£15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a Â£5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

News.title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
News.content:
Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.

Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.

Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.

Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.

The European benchmark natural gas price topped â¬75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.

The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.

Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.

Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased.

"The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top â¬80 by the end of this year.

Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up.

"We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.

Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying Â£1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast".

However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.

News.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
News.content:
Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving Â£1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with Â£37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

News.title: Burnham and Macron agree to scale up action on small boats
News.content:
Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."

The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum. He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, No 10 said Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

They also "discussed the UK's drive to get closer to Europe", while Burnham raised concerns about the potential impact of the Made in Europe procurement plan, being drawn up in Brussels to protect EU industries, on British sectors.

Burnham has previously called for closer ties with Europe, as had his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The pair also discussed establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the Scalp long-range missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile.

The leaders also discussed the situation in the Middle East and the need to ensure de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And Burnham raised Israel's move to open up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank, saying it was "unacceptable and only served to undermine the prospect of the two-state solution".

The development in the so-called E1 area would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Plans to build there have long been internationally condemned, with settlements illegal under international law.

The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.

But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.

France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.

And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.

The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

News.title: Canada unveils new $20 bill featuring portrait of King Charles
News.content:
Canada is the first Commonwealth country to put the King on its banknotes outside of Britain since his ascension to the throne.

In addition, it also depicts a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment", according to the Bank of Canada.

Wayne Long, a Liberal MP and secretary of state for the Canada Revenue Agency, said at the unveiling that the symbols on the banknote "serve as a powerful reminder of who we are as a nation and what we value."

Some elements of it were chosen in consultation with an Indigenous advisory council, the central bank added.

It is the second vertical banknote issued in Canada. The first is the $10 bill, depicting Black civil rights advocate Viola Desmond. Its design went on to be selected as best in the world in 2018 by the International Bank Note Society.

The new $20 banknote will enter circulation early next year, said Macklem.

Polling suggests that many Canadians believe the country should end its formal ties to the British monarchy, particularly in the French-speaking province of Quebec.

But the monarchy's popularity received a small bump, external as tensions rose between Canada and the US, including the ongoing US-Canada trade war and US President Donald Trump's comments about making Canada the "51st state".

Prime Minister Mark Carney invited the King to open Canada's parliament in May - a visit that Carney at the time said "clearly underscores the sovereignty of our country".

The King is Canada's head of state and is represented in Canada by its Governor General Louise Arbour.

News.title: Channel smuggling gangs resort to 'mega-dinghies' as crackdown limits small boat supply
News.content:
What they leave behind in Gravelines is a scene of dejection and exhaustion. A limp toddler is carried past me towards a police officer, who revives him with a light shake.

This all unfolds next to four or so men casting their fishing rods into the increasingly choppy waters. It is peak holiday season here. They and other dogwalkers barely glance at the crestfallen migrants wading back to the sand.

Before, the gangs would often launch boats in the dead of night, but with increased police patrols, charity workers tell us the gangs now see the middle of the day as a better opportunity, as it takes taxi boats longer to arrive and it allows them to better co-ordinate boarding.

"You feel guilty being there - going to the beach and having a good time, while these families are in such terrible situations," observes a woman with her young daughter. They had been playing with a bucket and spade.

"It's hard," she admits. "We regularly see people on the beach attempting the crossing. It feels like living in two parallel worlds that have nothing to do with each other; it's really strange."

The migrants remaining will wait for their next opportunity, as per their agreement with the gangs. But because of more robust policing that wait is now typically weeks, even months, rather than days.

They also need a favourable weather window: the wind needs to ideally be under 5 knots and waves need to be less than 0.8m for a small boat to have a chance of making it across.

To improve their chances of avoiding detection and to be closer to a taxi boat, charity workers tell us migrants are also sleeping closer to the beach in the woods or among the dunes, instead of at the larger camps where they can wash, or receive food, water and medication.

It is after arriving at the largest settlement at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, that we soon find ourselves in direct confrontation with the people smugglers.

As the intense heat bears down on a tent where people can charge their devices, we initially meet two young Egyptian men who are visibly tired and disheartened. They have been staying in squalid conditions for months and have made several unsuccessful attempts to cross.

"The police stopped us from leaving and destroyed the boats," explains one. He says he wants to go to the UK so he can work and obtain legal papers.

A young Sudanese woman and Afghan man also told us they had also tried to cross dozens of times. We have been to the camp on several occasions over the past year, but this time there was a perceptible unease.

Riot police had cleared out the tents in the same week, and the day before around 400 migrants preparing for a taxi boat in the nearby Hardelot forest were forced to return after several fires broke out.

It is evident the migrants and the gangs have been repeatedly frustrated, and the sight of our camera in one corner of the camp leads to us being attacked.

After we had agreed to stop filming, one smuggler, around 5'8" tall (172cm) and in a new grey tracksuit, tries to grab our camera. He then repeatedly throws rocks at us from close range, striking our cameraman above the eye.

News.title: Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers creator dies at 84
News.content:
The man behind the novelty pop act Jive Bunny and The Mastermixers has died aged 84, the company he founded has confirmed.

John Pickles formed Jive Bunny in Rotherham in 1989 and the act went on to have three UK number ones with Swing The Mood, That's What I Like and Let's Party.

Jive Bunny records typically used synthesisers and sampling to combine contemporary pop music with hits from the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s.

A statement from the Mastermix company described Pickles as "a true pioneer in the music industry", adding that he was "a leader, an entrepreneur, a businessman and an incredibly talented songwriter".

His "creativity, vision and passion for music touched the lives and careers of so many people around the world, and for the most fortunate of us, he was dad," the statement said.

Fox News have announced that they are parting ways with Fox Business host Maria Bartiromo with immediate effect.

In a brief statement, Fox said: “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”

Bartiromo was reportedly fired for sharing internal Fox News discussions with the White House.

In July, Fox News allegedly issued guidance to avoid diving into President Trump’s claims during a primetime speech that China meddled in the 2020 election, according to the media news outlet Status.

Bartiromo then shared a text message about the guidance with the White House, according to the outlet.

open image in gallery Maria Bartiromo has departed Fox with immediate effect ( Getty )

Fox News then got a call from the White House about the alleged disclosure, Puck reported, eventually prompting the network to pull Bartiromo from the air in August and later fire her.

The Independent has contacted the White House, Fox News and Bartiromo’s reported attorney for comment.

Bartiromo was known as a favorite of President Donald Trump, and had been linked to the vacant role of press secretary for the Trump administration following the departure of Karoline Leavitt.

However, Vanity Fair’s Washington Correspondent Aidan McLaughlin downplayed the suggestion on X, stating: “Bartiromo is not leaving for a job in the Trump admin, I’m told.”

Fox have announced that today’s Mornings with Maria will be the final episode. As of tomorrow, the show will be rebranded as Mornings with Fox Business and will be helmed by a rotating cast of anchors.

open image in gallery Bartiromo was reportedly fired after alerting the White House to a Fox News guidance urging reporters to avoid diving into President Trump’s recent claims of a Chinese election meddling conspiracy in 2020 ( AFP/Getty )

The Friday show Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street will also be rebranded as Fox Business Network's Wall Street, and will be hosted this week by Cheryl Casone.

This weekend’s Sunday Morning Futures will be hosted by Jason Chaffetz, with a new host set to be announced at a later date.

Bartiromo, who had become one of the network’s most prominent hosts over the last decade, was known as a vocal supporter of Trump.

In April, Trump told her during an interview that he was “very surprised” that crude oil prices were “only” at $92 per barrel and predicted that the war could “be over very soon.”

open image in gallery Bartiromo is a known favorite of Trump’s ( AFP/Getty )

“If you told me that we were going to be at only 92 a barrel, $92 a barrel, I would have been very surprised. All right, and you know what? I'm very happy, and it's going to come dropping down very big as soon as it's over,” he said.

Last June, Bartiromo received mockery after misleadingly sharing a fake Trump social media post.

During an interview with Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-TX) following the nationwide No Kings protest, Bartiromo quoted the fabricated post as she said: “I love the way the president handled it because, congressman, he put out a tweet. He writes: ‘A huge thank you to all the No Kings protesters yesterday. I was very concerned that a King was trying to take my place but thanks to your tireless efforts I am still your president! Great job all!’”

Turning back to Crenshaw, Bartiromo gleefully added: “The president had fun with that!”

People are being urged to nurture their pensions much like growing plants or vegetables.

It comes as new findings reveal that one in three adults (33 per cent) do not know what is inside their pension pot.

Additionally, more than half of those surveyed (52 per cent) admitted they have never checked their pension balance.

The study was commissioned by Pension Attention, an industry-led campaign coordinated jointly by the Association of British Insurers (ABI) and Pensions UK.

According to the research, which surveyed 2,000 UK adults via OnePoll in July and August, nearly three in 10 people (29 per cent) have no idea how much money they will require for retirement.

The initiative has explored several themes over the years, with its latest campaign securing support from giant vegetable growers.

Kevin Fortey, a Guinness World Record breaker who is also known as “Mr Giant Veg”, said: “One tiny seed, given enough time and a bit of care, can grow into something incredible. I think pensions are much the same.”

Pensions minister Torsten Bell said: “Some people love growing vegetables, but everyone should get involved with growing their pension savings.

“What you plant today shapes what you’ll harvest at retirement.

“So take a few minutes now to check in on your pension, your future self will thank you for it.”

Pensions minister Torsten Bell ( Jordan Pettitt/PA )
