World.title: Karabakh Revival Fund partners the first Lachin International Film Festival (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Karabakh Revival Fund (KRF) served as an official partner of the first Lachin International Film Festival, held in Lachin from 24 to 27 August.

The festival formed part of the ceremonial programme marking Lachin City Day and represents a further step in the cultural revival of Karabakh and East Zangezur.

Held under the banner “Where Film Meets LIFE”, it was organised by the Hoçazfilm studio with the support of the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Special Representative Office of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Lachin district, the Karabakh Revival Fund, the Film Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Bakı Abadlıq Xidməti.

As the first international film festival ever held in Karabakh and East Zangezur, it showed once again that the reconstruction of the liberated territories is not a matter of infrastructure alone: restoring the cultural and civic life of these lands is no less of a priority.

The festival will be remembered as more than a programme of screenings — it was a cultural event that embodied the idea of revival itself. Its significance works on several levels at once: it brings new creative voices to light, introduces Lachin’s cultural revival to an international audience, and establishes the city as a new creative venue on the map of world cinema.

Among those attending were government officials, prominent figures from culture and the arts, guests from abroad, and residents and visitors of Lachin.

Speaking at the ceremony, Rahman Hajiyev, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Karabakh Revival Fund, said that alongside the large-scale reconstruction under way across the liberated territories, bringing cultural life back to the region remains a particular priority.

The festival, he said, gives filmmakers from Azerbaijan and abroad a rare chance to see Karabakh as it is today. He expressed confidence that the initiative will inspire the international film community with the story of the region — its past and its present revival — and encourage filmmakers to take up Karabakh as a subject in future work.

Close to 300 films from 47 countries were submitted to the festival, of which 20 titles representing 15 countries were selected for screening. Among them was a special Karabakh premiere of the Uzbek film Amir Temur, directed by Jacob Schwartz.

The closing and awards ceremony was held as part of a special event for Lachin City Day, attended by hundreds of residents and visitors. Official Selection certificates were presented to 39 participants, and 17 awards were made in total. The festival’s official prize, the Golden Oak Branch, went to five Azerbaijani and two international directors.

World.title: Traditional owners say national park can 'breathe again' after handback
World.content:
After decades of fighting to reclaim their ancestral land, traditional owners say Boodjamulla National Park can finally "breathe again" now that it is being returned.

About a 4-hour drive north-west of Mount Isa, Boodjamulla is one of outback Queensland's most popular national parks, drawing more than 20,000 visitors each year to sites such as Lawn Hill Gorge and the World Heritage-listed Riversleigh fossil deposits.

Today, more than 247,000 hectares of Boodjamulla will be formally returned to the Waanyi people, who have maintained a connection to the country for more than 30,000 years.

Boodjamulla National Park is about a 4-hour drive north-west of Mount Isa. (supplied: Waanyi PBC)

Hayley Iles, chair of the Waanyi Prescribed Body Corporate (PBC), which represents traditional owners, said the handback felt like "a long-awaited homecoming".

"The land breathes again," Ms Iles said.

"Our elders fought very long to let everyone know that this is our country. This is our land. This is where we do our practices.

"To be sanctioned by the white man to say that's ours, is important … I think there's going to probably be a little bit of crying."

Hayley Iles says Boodjamulla being handed back feels like a "homecoming". (ABC News: Tim Little)

Boodjamulla, meaning rainbow serpent country, is known for its deep gorges and flowing water, which cut through the surrounding plains.

After being dispossessed of their land, generations of Waanyi people endured long and often bitter fights for recognition of their country.

In 1994, Waanyi people and other native title groups staged a three-week sit in at Boodjamulla, demanding greater say in the management of the park and nearby Century Mine.

Lawn Hill Gorge made headlines when it was used in Tourism Australia's Crocodile Dundee ad campaign. (Supplied: Tourism & Events Queensland)

Ms Iles said the protest, followed by another in 2002, helped build momentum.

"Our elders negotiated with people from Carpentaria Land Council, lawyers, anthropologists to get royalty payments out of Century Mine," she said.

"That was the start of it."

Formal negotiations between the Waanyi Native Title Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland government began in 2020, paving the way for the park's return.

The land was progressively transferred in three stages, with the final tranche completed in January this year.

Boodjamulla was converted from a cattle station to a national park in 1984, before being expanded in 1992. (Supplied: Waanyi PBC)

Department of Tourism, Science and Innovation executive director Karrell Ross said the agreement required the park to be leased back to the state.

"There are other models, but this one is very unique … part of the … [agreement] is funding in perpetuity," Ms Ross said.

"So, there is still a responsibility for the department and still a responsibility for Waanyi PBC.

"We've got a board of management with equal representation … it's about working together."

Boodjamulla National Park has been leased back to the state government to ensure ongoing access for visitors. (Supplied: Qld Department of Environment and Science)

Ms Ross said visitors travelling to the national park should not expect any "huge changes" to access or services.

The significant change was the land was recognised as Aboriginal land, Ms Ross said.

"You'll see both Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service and Waanyi rangers working together, sharing their knowledge, the Waanyi people sharing their cultural knowledge of the area and QPWS also sharing their knowledge about managing land."

Waanyi people have ancestral ties to Boodjamulla dating back more than 30,000 years. (Supplied: Waanyi PBC)

For Ms Iles, today's ceremony represents a triumph following immense work, and a reminder of the time it all took.

"I have family travelling from New South Wales and the Northern Territory … families are coming from all over, so I am jumping out of my skin," she said.

"There is a bit of sadness, because there was a lot of our elders that fought for us to be doing what we're going to be doing [today], who are now gone.

"It is a testament to the resilience, patience and enduring spirit of our elders and our ancestors."

World.title: Brisbane man charged with alleged supply of gel blaster guns interstate
World.content:
A Brisbane man has been charged with allegedly supplying gel blaster firearms to customers around the country.

The Heathwood man, 38, was charged with two counts of taking or sending a firearm or firearm part across borders and will face the Brisbane Magistrate's Court today.

The maximum penalty for the offence is 10 years imprisonment.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) first began investigations after discovering gel blasters while searching a home in Isabella Plains in the ACT in 2022.

Using information obtained during the search, the AFP said it was able to develop an "intelligence profile" on the scale and scope of gel blaster firearms being distributed around Australia.

Gel blasters sold online raise concerns among gun safety advocates Gel blasters sold in Queensland are legal but experts warn they carry a serious cross-border legal risk as other states crack down.

Gel blasters are classified as prohibited weapons in every state and territory except Queensland and it is illegal to transfer firearms or firearm parts through the postal system.

In August 2025, AFP officers and the Queensland Police Service searched businesses in Brisbane and Toowoomba allegedly linked to the interstate supply of gel blasters.

AFP Detective Superintendent Jen Cullen said gel blasters pose a "significant risk" to the public and law enforcement because they can be used to create fear, intimidate or commit crimes.

"Anyone not living in Queensland who has a gel blaster is urged to surrender it to police immediately. Illegally possessing a gel blaster can be met with severe legal ramifications," she said.

"The AFP takes matters involving gel blasters seriously and have the resources to identify offenders who seek to profit from the sale or distribution of these items."

World.title: Americans urge caution as Australia braces for data centre boom
World.content:
As a dominatrix drag queen struts through a crowd with her eyes set on tackling corporate greed, she uses brute force to throw aside actors portraying the tech giants locals blame for rising power prices.

It's an unusual display of theatrics, aimed at firing up fed-up residents of North Carolina, on the east coast of the United States, who say data centres are driving up their power bills, before they are even built.

On the front steps of a Durham courthouse in June, hundreds of community members lined up to voice their concerns about a proposed 18 per cent rise in their electricity bills, which they blamed on new infrastructure needed for data centres.

A chorus, led by local activists The Raging Grannies, led the group in song.

"The people or the parasites, which side are you on? We're singing to you profiteers so hear us loud and clear. We won't stand idly by while you kill all that we hold dear," they sang.

The Raging Grannies protest about power hikes. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

It is a show of support against what the protesters say is corporate greed.

But when it comes to data centres in the US, it is not just the environment and human health locals were concerned about.

The opposition to data centres at the rally was also ideological, with protesters against the storing of surveillance material, and artificial intelligence taking jobs.

They are all arguments about an industry which has grown from about 3,000 data centres in 2021 to about 4,000 in 2026, according to the World Resources Institute.

Liz Hutchby protested about bills and the environment. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

Noise, diesel concerns

The Drag Down Our Electric Bills Rally attracted hundreds of peaceful protesters, who said big tech was responsible for their growing bills.

Duke Energy, the privately owned power company that generates and supplies electricity to consumers, applied to the North Carolina utilities commissioner to increase prices by 18 per cent.

Prior to a repeal of tax incentives in July, data centre companies in North Carolina paid no tax on their electricity usage as a drawcard to attract investment.

It is now home to about 90 data centres and successfully brought companies Apple, Meta and Google south of Virginia, the data centre capital.

The actual power price rises for North Carolina are still under negotiation and are yet to be signed off by the utilities commission.

Carl Hintz is a local school teacher. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

Local science teacher Carl Hintz was part of the protest.

"This electric company is making the argument they need to produce even more electricity to be able to power these data centres," he said.

"Even though these data centres haven't been built yet, it's already impacting people with higher electricity bills because of the anticipation that it might be built."

Lynne Taylor lives two hours away in Charlotte, where there are about 35 data centres, according to the international Data Center Map.

She said she was concerned about regional data centres taking up agricultural land alongside noise, health and environmental impacts.

She was also opposed to AI replacing jobs.

"What we have learned in America is that [you're] more likely to get kicked by a kangaroo than see any real economic gain for citizens," Mrs Taylor said.

"The developers of data centres promise many jobs for humans, but frankly, the majority of jobs are not being fulfilled."

Lynne Taylor is concerned about potential environmental and health impacts of data centres. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

A new frontier

As Australia straps in to connect more data centres to the electricity grid and water supplies, residents and academics in the United States are warning governments should take heed of what they have learned.

According to the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO), there are 165 data centres operating across the country, with another 225 in development.

By 2036, AEMO says data centres will account for 13 per cent of the country's power usage.

Advocates say it is Australia's chance to get in front and take advantage of companies needing quick turnaround times and the money they have to spend.

There are 225 new data centres in development across Australia. (Supplied: Microsoft)

Eric Masanet is a professor at the University of California in Santa Barbara, specialising in emerging technologies.

He said the Australian government could draw on America's experience to legislate to ensure companies were transparent about what they are doing, how they are operating and the resources they are using.

"One challenge we faced in the US is that data centre builds are being announced every week, they're huge, but they're behind a veil of secrecy," Professor Masanet said.

" There's very little transparency between the industry and the communities that will host these data centres and the policymakers who are either working with the industry or seeking to regulate them. "

He said the lack of transparency fuelled community pushback.

Eric Masanet says Australian policy needs to make sure data centre companies are transparent. (Supplied: University of California)

"They don't know how much water, how much air pollution will be associated with that data centre down the street because the companies won't share the data," Professor Masanet said.

"It's often hidden behind a non-disclosure agreement and if local officials are aware, they've entered into these NDAs where they're not sharing with the public."

Professor Masanet's laboratory tracks emerging US policies relating to data centres.

He said some states were tough with bans or moratoriums and others, like Texas, were incentivising them without guardrails, but there was little middle ground.

He believes Australia could take heed and be tough, while making the most of investment in renewable energy projects.

The federal government is already introducing rules requiring data centres to fund new renewable energy to offset their usage, with exemptions for Queensland and the Northern Territory to use fossil fuels.

In construction, data centres could bring hundreds of jobs.

But to run them, only a handful of people are needed, depending on the size.

Protesters rally against electricity price hikes. (Supplied: Celeste Guajardo WUNC News)

Boom potential

Simon Currie, founder of energy strategy company Energy Estate, said Australia should take advantage of the eagerness of developers to build data centres.

"How do we leverage this to deliver on all of the other things that we need to build out the economy for the next 50 to 100 years?" Mr Currie said.

He said they needed to be built in the right spot, near a reliable electricity supply.

Mr Currie believes data centres could pay for a portion of Victoria's renewable energy transition.

"They want the power, we want offshore wind," he said, referring to Victoria's plan to develop an offshore wind industry.

"How about we twin things together?"

Simon Currie says Australia needs to be smart about its policy around data centres. (Supplied: Energy Estate)

He said concerns about noise and resource use could be addressed by requiring the companies to invest in the best technology, which he said could be the difference between noisy, resource-guzzling data centres and those that go unnoticed.

Mr Currie believes co-locating data centres with industries that need the heat they produce could result in an uptick in manufacturing and jobs.

"We've got food insecurity and we're losing food manufacturers because they were used to cheap gas," he said.

"How do we use industries like data centres to lever in and support other industries?"

Newsgathering for this story occurred as part of a study tour funded through a Rural Press Club of Victoria scholarship.

World.title: Shire confirms five dogs poisoned on two streets, killing three
World.content:
The RSPCA is investigating a spate of dog poisonings in Western Australia's Gascoyne, after five pets became unwell and three died.

The Shire of Carnarvon, 900 kilometres north of Perth, confirmed the five dogs were poisoned on two streets within the town.

"Sadly, three of those dogs found in Morgan Way passed away," Shire of Carnarvon executive manager Stefan Louw said.

Phoenix one of the lucky ones

Carnarvon dog owner Melinda Sattell recalls the heartbreaking moment she realised her four-legged family member Phoenix had been poisoned in their own backyard.

"She started foaming at the mouth and at this point we went 'she's been baited'," Ms Sattell said.

On the way to the vet, Phoenix was barely conscious and when they arrived Ms Sattell was told her dog only had minutes left to live.

Melinda Sattell says since the poisoning Phoenix is now scared to travel in the car and be out around new people. (ABC Pilbara/Rachel Hagan)

"It was heartbreaking. Your best friend is in your arms, and you may not be able to save them," she said.

"It's not fair on the dogs or the families who go through it, it's very hard to explain to a child why their dog suddenly isn't well and may die."

Ms Sattell said the family was rocked by the incident that happened at their own property but thankful Phoenix was able to make a full recovery.

"We thought she was just playing with her tennis ball but it wasn't a tennis ball, she had eaten something she had found in the corner of the yard," she said.

She said Phoenix had consumed a poisoned sausage, and within about 20 minutes of eating the meat began to shake.

Warning for dog owners

The incidents occurred in late August and at the time, Carnarvon's Coral Coast Veterinary Hospital posted on social media warning others about the suspected poisoning.

The veterinary hospital had treated five pets from three different households that had symptoms of organophosphate poisoning within 48 hours.

The post advised residents to look out for hypersalivation, constricted pupils, shaking and diarrhoea.

Coral Coast Veterinary Hospital has urged pet owners to be vigilant after the suspected baiting. (ABC Pilbara:Rachel Hagan)

Mr Louw said dogs should be kept on a leash outside and owners should be wary of what they are sniffing or eating off the ground.

The RSPCA confirmed it is investigating.

Lasting toll

For Phoenix's family her recovery has been miraculous, but has also come at a cost of about $3,000.

Ms Sattell said it had set her family back six months financially.

"I would never part with my pets unless I was that broke that there was no funds available," she said.

"I am just lucky to have a stable job," she said.

If the perpetrator is found, Ms Sattell said they should be forced to repay all of the victims' vet bills and compensation for the stress it caused to owners.

Phoenix is on the road to recovery and getting back to her busy life of long walks and burying bones. (ABC Pilbara: Rachel Hagan)

"Now my dogs don't go into my backyard without someone with them, and they are on leads at all times," she said.

"I previously thought my backyard was safe for my dogs, but I've been proven wrong."

World.title: US vice-president says Iran conflict not a war
World.content:
US Vice-President JD Vance says he would not categorise the Iran conflict as a war despite continuing clashes with Tehran.

Mr Vance's comments come amid signs that US President Donald Trump was trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.

"I wouldn't call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting," Mr Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by US midterm elections in November.

He said he recognised there "had been places where this has flared up", but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

"But when you ask, 'When will this end?' you're asking me a question like, 'When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?'" Mr Vance said.

"I think the reality is I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians."

After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with US raids on Sunday, local time, deepening the impasse while Iran maintains its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran launched missiles and drones overnight at a US base in Kuwait following the war's biggest escalation in more than a month.

Kuwait's military said its air defences had intercepted missiles and drones, but following that, the war's biggest flare-up since July appeared to subside, with no more major attacks from either side reported since.

The US has more than 50,000 troops in the Middle East. The Trump administration has significantly increased assets into the region, including nearly 20 warships focused on a blockade.

In some instances, troops have been deployed for longer than expected and have been pulled from Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

Mr Vance insisted the US would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial ships.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Republicans control of Congress, the Trump administration has been pushing the message that the flow of oil through the waterway is returning to prewar levels.

"Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone," Mr Vance said of Iran.

"If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now it's almost back to where it was before the conflict even started."

JD Vance says the flow of oil is almost back to pre-war levels. (Reuters)

Mr Trump's approval rating has sunk close to a record low as the president, who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars, finds himself in a quagmire.

Eighteen US troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr Trump was now discussing with senior aides whether to declare the Iran war over. Last week he posted a photo of a banner that said "Mission Accomplished".

Iran said on Thursday it hit US military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, although the UAE reported no such attack, in retaliation to a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.

Iran labels US strike on wedding a 'war crime' Iranian officials are comparing the incident to a strike on a girl's school on the first night of the war which killed 160 people.

Mr Vance said the United States was investigating the strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

"We're investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know," he said.

"When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.

"I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far, so I'm extremely sceptical of this."

US Central Command spokesman Tim Hawkins previously said the US military was looking into the reports.

A boy lies wounded in hospital after the strike Iranian authorities say hit a house hosting a wedding. (Reuters via Razieh Poudat/ISNA/WANA)

On Thursday it was reported on Iranian state television that a 22-year-old woman had died in hospital following the strike that hit a home during the wedding, taking the total reported death toll to five.

Iranian officials said nearly 70 people were wounded.

Iranian state media broadcast footage of a funeral for the victims on Thursday, showing mourners carrying caskets and gathering outside the village of Kuhestak in Sirik County.

"If it was a military location, it wouldn't be so painful. This was a wedding ceremony, but they turned people's joy into mourning," the semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted a local man as saying.

AFP/Reuters/AP

World.title: Australian wildcard stuns Italian star in US Open boilover
World.content:
Dane Sweeny has won a real-life David-versus-Goliath battle to rock the US Open with a stunning second-round upset over dual grand slam semi-finalist Lorenzo Musetti.

The unheralded Australian wildcard took down the 14th seed 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 on Friday morning (AEST) for the biggest win of his career.

Standing only 170cm high, Sweeny rose to the occasion to reach the third round of a grand slam for the first time and earn a minimum pay day of $US290,000 ($A402,750).

For a couple of heady hours it looked like his underdog countrymen Tristan Schoolkate and Alexei Popyrin would join Sweeny in round three.

Osaka, Keys mount thrilling fightbacks Naomi Osaka wobbled through the second set to fight back and beat Kateřina Siniaková in three, while Madison Keys staved off five match points to keep her US Open dreams alive on day of high drama at Flushing Meadows.

But Schoolkate's inspired run from qualifying finally came to a halt at the hands of fifth-seeded French Open runner-up Flavio Cobilli.

Schoolkate snatched the first set before the Italian showed his class to prevail 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 after two hours and 41 minutes in New York's scorching summer heat.

And two years after upstaging Novak Djokovic in the US Open's third round, Popyrin fell short of a place in the last 32 once again, losing a tense four-set battle with Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Like Schoolkate, Popyrin took the opening set before the 25th-seeded South American claimed two pivotal tiebreakers, then the match 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to seal a likely third-round date with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

But ranked more than 100 places below his world number 14 opponent, Sweeny is savouring a mighty breakthrough after bossing Musetti into submission.

He ran the 14th seed ragged and had the Italian looking in particular distress when he required a medical time-out after falling behind a double break at 0-3 in the all-important third set.

Even after clawing one break back, Musetti — who has made the Wimbledon and French Open semi-finals over the past two years — continued remonstrating animatedly to his courtside box.

Despite sporting a massive ice pack on his right elbow after his first-round win, Sweeny continued diving like Boris Becker for acrobatic winning volleys at the net.

And the 25-year-old was duly rewarded with a last-32 shot at another Italian, world number 22 Luciano Daredri on Saturday (AEST) — and a rankings rise to a career-best 115 in the world, or better.

"I'm just grateful to be even able to compete in grand slams. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster," Sweeny said.

"And to soak up the atmosphere and get a win, a couple of wins, in front of this crowd, is awesome."

Australia's sixth seed Alex de Minaur was scheduled to play Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp on The Grandstand after Schoolkate's match.

AAP

World.title: Fox makes golden return to Paris Olympic venue
World.content:
Jess Fox has made a triumphant return to the Vaires-sur-Marne Nautical Stadium on the outskirts of Paris, claiming yet another gold medal in the ICF Canoe Slalom World Cup series.

Returning to the venue where she won two Olympic gold medals in 2024, Fox was once again unstoppable in the K1 event.

The now five-time world champion even overcame a two-second penalty to top the standings for her second World Cup win of the season.

"I have great memories here in Paris. It's always a pleasure to race here with the amazing crowd," Fox said in a bilingual post-race interview.

"The course was hard. It was very challenging, very physical — I'm still out of breath.

"I gave it everything and I'm so happy to take the win today."

Noémie Fox finished fifth, just one-tenth of a second off the podium. (Supplied: Romain Bruneau)

Fox, who was born in Marseille and is the daughter of French 1996 Olympic bronze medallist Myriam Fox-Jerusalmi, claimed victory by 0.73 seconds from Slovakian Eliška Mintálová, who was the only paddler in the top six to complete a clean run and not suffer a penalty.

Paris Olympic silver medallist Klaudia Zwolińska of Poland finished third, edging Ukraine's Viktoriia Us out of the medals by just 0.05 seconds.

Fox came into the event off the back of winning three gold medals at the world championships in Oklahoma, capping a superb comeback season after she had surgery to remove a tumour from her kidney nine months ago.

Noémie Fox, who enjoyed her own golden moment on the Vaires-sur-Marne course in 2024, was a further 0.05 seconds back in fifth.

In the men's event, Australian Lucien Delfour finished in 10th place, having been hit with four seconds' worth of penalties, while Italian Giovanni de Gennaro claimed gold with a clean run.

The Fox's will have another chance to win gold in the C1 event, set to take place Friday night (AEST), an event where Jess has won back-to-back Olympic golds in Tokyo and Paris.

World.title: Venue apologises for AI flyers that have 'no place' in creative industry
World.content:
Chloe Young is sick to death of seeing images generated by artificial intelligence (AI) in their online feeds.



"You scroll and scroll and scroll, and it all looks the same," said the 28-year-old creative who runs an online sewing and garment-making business.

Young is facing an uphill battle amid a global AI boom pushed by billions of dollars in investment and free or relatively cheap access for consumers.

Closer to home, governments are fast-tracking applications for a growing number of data centres, while grappling with how to manage their vast power and water demands.

Chloe Young is not a graphic designer but felt compelled to do something to push back. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

For Young, putting coloured pen to paper is a deliberate rejection of AI's ability to generate "content" in the form of text, music, video and imagery.

'Homogeneous' social feeds

In response, Young put out a call on social media to design posters for small businesses and community groups in Toowoomba for a small fee, or free if they could not afford it.

While that may be more expensive and take much longer than AI tools, Young said they felt they needed to push back against the "hollow", "soulless" and "homogeneous" AI-generated posters flooding social media feeds.

Chloe Young is putting pen to paper to make the posters. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

"I just got so frustrated with everything and everyone that I said, like, 'Hey, I will literally do anything for $5 or free,'" Young said.

Despite not being a graphic designer, Young said within days of posting the call-out, they had received nearly 30 inquiries from people looking for alternatives to AI-generated content.

Young said seeing businesses rely on AI immediately puts them off using their goods or services.

"I can't tell the difference between a local business and a community event anymore because everything has the same look," they said.

Their biggest concern is the impact on artists and creative work.

"Art is meant to make you feel something," Young said.

"AI feels hollow. It doesn't bring feeling; it brings a lack of feeling."

Author pushback

Just a few streets away from Young's sewing studio, Taylor Hailes said she felt pushback against AI while preparing to open her boutique wine bar and bookshop, The Book Pour.

Book Pour owner Taylor Hailes never expected to need an AI policy for her bricks-and-mortar venue. (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

In the frantic days before opening, Ms Hailes said she turned to AI for help drawing up flyers and social media posts.

"When you're in a small business, and you're trying to do everything at once, you naturally turn to tools that can help you out," she said.

" I put together some AI-generated posters, which you see a lot of at the moment. "

But Ms Hailes said after posting the promotional material, she received a call from one of the authors, who had recently withdrawn from another event elsewhere because of its use of AI.

"[The author] reached out and asked about our AI policy," she said.

"That's when I realised I didn't actually know enough to understand what the issue was at its core."

Ms Hailes said the conversation prompted her to learn more about how AI works and the risks it posed to creative industries.

The Book Pour's AI policy states, "AI has no place in the creative industry". (ABC Southern Queensland: Dan McCray)

She said she had not realised generative AI systems are trained using material already available online.

"I could totally see where they were coming from and why they wanted to protect the creative arts sector," Ms Hailes said.

Taylor Haile's business posted an apology statement on her business's Instagram after learning more about AI. (supplied)

Many generative AI systems are trained on collections of copyrighted material, which differs between companies and models.

The ABC has also reported that second-hand booksellers have been getting orders for rare and out-of-print books from companies working for tech giants, sparking fears AI could be ingesting then destroying printed work.

Earning goodwill

These realisations ultimately led Ms Hailes to introduce an AI policy and apologise for any harm she may have caused.

"It's about working with indie authors and making sure there's no AI used in their work, no AI used in the artwork, and making sure the work we do here doesn't use it either," she said.

She said the move had earned her goodwill.

"We made sure our community knew what had happened, what had been brought to our attention and what we were going to do about it," she said.

"We had a really great response."

Park Thaichon, an associate professor of marketing at the University of Southern Queensland, said the concerns reflected a broader shift among some consumers.

While AI can be a cost-effective and time-efficient way to create content, he said some people were becoming wary of its growing use because "it can look too boring, and there's nothing new or outside the box at all".

Australia's largest data centre in regional Queensland has just been proposed roughly 120 kilometres west of Toowoomba. (Supplied: Urbis)

He said consumers were particularly concerned when businesses used AI-generated images of people or were not transparent about their use of the technology.

"This type of thing can lead to misunderstanding, and people will lose trust," he said.

Meanwhile, Young said they felt the heavy adoption of AI seemed unnecessary in some cases and overlooked what could become a less-human future.

"We don't see the problem until it's problematic," they said.

"I know someone can look at (my posters) and be like 'wow, squiggles,' but at least I know that AI didn't make that."

World.title: The rise of the ‘fridge red’: Three red wines perfect for chilling (from $28)
World.content:
When your room resembles the inside of a parked hatchback in January, it makes no sense to serve red wine at room temp. Some are even made for chilling down, here’s why.

Red wine has spent far too long sitting at the serious end of the drinks table waiting patiently for someone to explain why it shouldn’t be allowed near an Esky. We chill beer, white wine, rosé and sparkling, yet suggest cooling a red and someone inevitably appears in a blazer with elbow patches to defend centuries of tradition. Somehow red wine has escaped one of the greatest inventions in human history: refrigeration.

Revenge, and these red wines, are best served cold. Dion Georgopoulos

For generations, we’ve been told to serve red wine at “room temperature”, advice that might make sense in European castles, but in Australia, where room temperature can resemble the inside of a parked hatchback in January, the instruction feels less useful.

Red wine is often served too warm, and that warmth leaves it tasting soupy, boozy and a little blurry. A light chill brightens fruit, sharpens freshness and ups the refreshment factor.

Of course, nobody is suggestion putting your dusty bottle of Penfold’s Grange next to the ice-cream tub. This is more about knocking a chill into the light to medium red wine varieties and styles that are increasingly in vogue.

World.title: Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeTrump diplomacy Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash David Crowe Updated September 4, 2026 — 9:32am ,first published 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A casual remark from Donald Trump has heightened concerns in Britain about its military capacity after the US president seemed to dismiss the idea of helping one of America’s closest allies. Trump suggested the UK would not get his help in the event of a clash with Argentina over their rival claims to the Falkland Islands, where the two countries went to war in 1982. Trump has repeatedly linked the island dispute to the UK declining to send ships to help open the Strait of Hormuz. Bloomberg The president linked the issue to the Iran war by noting, as he has in the past, that former British prime minister Keir Starmer turned down his request for military support to help open the Strait of Hormuz. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told broadcaster GB News.



While Trump’s comments were brief and did not constitute a formal shift in foreign policy, they added to the debate in Britain over a potential conflict with Argentina, as its leader is becoming increasingly assertive about the territorial claim. Related Article FIFA World Cup ‘Build up the Royal Navy’: UK brawls over Falklands war after World Cup loss to Argentina Argentine President Javier Milei, one of Trump’s ideological allies and the beneficiary of generous White House support, this week declared the islands were a “sacred” claim for his country. Hours after Trump spoke, news emerged from Argentina suggesting Milei wanted to impose sanctions on British oil companies seeking to develop resources near the islands. The move could provoke Britain over the sovereignty of the waters, even though the Sea Lion field is not due to produce any oil until 2028.



Trump has helped Milei before. The White House approved a $US20 billion currency swap with Argentina last year to help stabilise the peso. That contrasted with Trump’s regular complaints about European allies such as the UK. Now there is speculation that Trump will support Milei in laying claim to oil fields around the Falklands because the US could get a share of the action. When GB News asked Trump if he would back Britain in any dispute, the US president praised the UK for winning the 1982 war but cast doubt on whether he would help in another conflict. British paratroopers march across East Falkland island during the 1982 war. Hulton Archive “I was there when they had the first war, that was a long time ago, and I watched it so carefully,” he said.



“And you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly. Related Article Middle East at war The US warship that spent too much time at sea finally gets a break “But it’s a long way away. That’s a big trip. It’s a long way. “So, your country’s not doing well. Don’t forget you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me. Your country was not there to help me.” Trump made the complaint while also repeating his previous claim that the US did not need help from Britain in the war with Iran. He said he asked Starmer if the UK could send a “couple of ships” and was told the UK had none to spare.



The formal US policy on the conflict is to remain neutral on the rival claims. Under the Monroe Doctrine, declared two centuries ago, US administrations see the Americas as their own sphere of influence, not a domain for European powers. Under Trump, the “Donroe Doctrine” dictates that America comes first. And the US president will only help those who give him what he wants – whether it is Greenland or a fleet of ships in the Persian Gulf. While the US said it was neutral in the 1982 war, it leaned toward Britain when Argentina’s military junta ordered an invasion of the islands. US president Ronald Reagan kept up supplies of military material to the UK when British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, sent a fleet to the South Atlantic to reclaim the formal British territory. The British victory was followed by the crumbling of the Argentine military dictatorship, under which an estimated 30,000 people were murdered, and many others were targeted in human rights abuses over eight years.



The Royal Navy had almost 200 vessels at the time of the Falklands War, while it has about 70 today, including some that are being decommissioned. MPs have warned in a series of reports that the country needs a stronger military. Labour MP Tan Dhesi, the chair of the House of Commons defence committee, this week urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to spend more on defence, and he named concerns about the US as one of the reasons. Trump with Argentine President Javier Milei in January, who is seem as one of his major ideological allies. Bloomberg “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority,” Dhesi told parliament. “That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later.”



Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Burnham’s office has issued a statement that repeats the British claim to the Falklands, which have been British territory since 1833 and were first sighted by an English captain in 1592. There were no indigenous inhabitants. The great unknown is how far Milei will go to provoke Britain. He is unpopular at home because his economic vision has failed to generate enough results for the public after decades of hardship. And he faces an election next year, which means he will be desperate enough to resort to patriotic fervour over the islands in the hope it can lift his stocks. Would he start a serious fight? Would he send forces to disrupt oil drilling in contested waters? Would he risk a conflict? That would be utterly irrational.



Even so, the 1982 war has a lesson that still applies today. Some leaders are quite capable of starting stupid wars. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Everyone’s fighting for spots’: This production factory woke a slumbering NRL giant
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Everyone’s fighting for spots’: This production factory woke a slumbering NRL giant Nick Wright September 4, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Kristian Woolf first took the coaching reins at the Dolphins, he was less concerned about what the top squad looked like and more curious about what was under the hood. Before taking the hot seat from inaugural coach Wayne Bennett, he was determined to ensure Redcliffe was a talent factory that would inspire sustainable success – much like the all-conquering Penrith Panthers. That idea dictated his early conversations with Dolphins CEO Terry Reader and Bennett. Once he heard of the involvement of Kurt Richards – who spent 13 years with the Brisbane Broncos and led the Queensland Maroons under-16s, 18s and 19s – Woolf was confident to sign on. Kristian Woolf was eager for a strong development pathway to be put in place ahead of recruitment. NRL Photos “It’s definitely something I was interested in. One of my first conversations with Terry and Wayne was about what we were doing with our academies and who was in charge of that,” Woolf said.



“When I knew that Kurt Richards was in charge of it, I knew we were in good hands, and it was a big part of me wanting to come to the club. When you’ve got those things right, and you’ve got the right people there, you tend to be able to build things for the future.” Related Article Updated

State of Origin ‘I needed to make a change’: The fall and rise of Boyd to Maroons’ top job In the early days, Reader foresaw the side’s fourth season would be the one where the fruits of their academy began to ripen. He was right. Winger Tevita Naufahu and versatile edge forward Brian Pouniu – whose first chance in the back row yielded 179 running metres and 39 tackles against the Eels – have become the maiden graduates of the academy, with lock Lewis Symonds and hooker John Fineanganofo also earning debuts.



Naufahu and Pouniu will take on the Gold Coast Titans on Friday night, with Selwyn Cobbo and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki rested to nurse niggling injuries. “We were obviously really impressed with how he played last time, and what I liked about his performance was he got better as the game went on. He got more and more confident and realised he’s right up to that level,” Woolf said of Pouniu, adding Naufahu had been “one of our best players every time he’s played for us”. A plethora of talent is yet to be tapped into at the top level. Those future hopefuls include two sons of former NRL stars – Noah Fien, whose father Nathan is an assistant at the Dolphins, and Adaquix Luke, whose dad Issac became a South Sydney legend – as well as preseason trial finds Zac Garton (back row) and LJ Nonu (wing). In last year’s maiden NRLQ under-21s series the Dolphins were undefeated, before finishing second in the expanded 12-round competition in 2026, when they finished top of the table, before losing the grand final to the Cowboys 24-22.



“We’ve got a good patch of young blokes coming through, and they challenge us all the time,” Dolphins lock Kurt Donoghoe said. “I think that’s definitely helping out a lot, it makes our training sessions better and the older boys try a little harder. “Everyone’s fighting for spots, everyone’s fighting for each other’s positions. Brian had his debut earlier in the year, and in his second game you could just tell how much better he was for that. Loading “They’ve got so much potential and are really comfortable they can jump in and do a job when we need them.”



Across the club’s opening three seasons, depth had ultimately proven the Dophins’ greatest obstacle. Despite entering the mid-point of the campaigns entrenched in the top eight, they quickly faded as injuries and suspensions cruelled their cause. There has been no such issue in their top-four 2026 finish, with Naufahu starring in the absence of Cobbo, and Pouniu’s breakout performance coming as Connelly Lemuelu fought back from a hamstring issue. Related Article Exclusive

A-League Women Meet the youngest coach in Australian history on a quest to be ‘best ever’ “I think it does make a difference,” Woolf said. “I look at our squad, and Max Plath plays 50 games this week, a couple of weeks ago it was Jack Bostock, a couple of weeks before that it was Kurt Donoghoe. We’ve got a nucleus of guys there who all debuted at this club. “They’ve all become first-graders at this club, some of those have gone on and played representative footy, they all love playing together – you can see when they’re on the field, there’s a real care factor for each other.



“That’s what we want the club to be about. We put a lot of time and effort and finances into our academy to make sure it’s strong and to make sure we’ve got good young players coming through who are well-developed, well-coached, and know what it means to be a Dolphins player.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The rise of the ‘fridge red’: Three red wines perfect for chilling (from $28)
World.content:
When your room resembles the inside of a parked hatchback in January, it makes no sense to serve red wine at room temp. Some are even made for chilling down, here’s why.

Red wine has spent far too long sitting at the serious end of the drinks table waiting patiently for someone to explain why it shouldn’t be allowed near an Esky. We chill beer, white wine, rosé and sparkling, yet suggest cooling a red and someone inevitably appears in a blazer with elbow patches to defend centuries of tradition. Somehow red wine has escaped one of the greatest inventions in human history: refrigeration.

Revenge, and these red wines, are best served cold. Dion Georgopoulos

For generations, we’ve been told to serve red wine at “room temperature”, advice that might make sense in European castles, but in Australia, where room temperature can resemble the inside of a parked hatchback in January, the instruction feels less useful.

Red wine is often served too warm, and that warmth leaves it tasting soupy, boozy and a little blurry. A light chill brightens fruit, sharpens freshness and ups the refreshment factor.

Of course, nobody is suggestion putting your dusty bottle of Penfold’s Grange next to the ice-cream tub. This is more about knocking a chill into the light to medium red wine varieties and styles that are increasingly in vogue.

World.title: Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeTrump diplomacy Trump suggests he would not help UK in another Falklands clash David Crowe Updated September 4, 2026 — 9:32am ,first published 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A casual remark from Donald Trump has heightened concerns in Britain about its military capacity after the US president seemed to dismiss the idea of helping one of America’s closest allies. Trump suggested the UK would not get his help in the event of a clash with Argentina over their rival claims to the Falkland Islands, where the two countries went to war in 1982. Trump has repeatedly linked the island dispute to the UK declining to send ships to help open the Strait of Hormuz. Bloomberg The president linked the issue to the Iran war by noting, as he has in the past, that former British prime minister Keir Starmer turned down his request for military support to help open the Strait of Hormuz. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told broadcaster GB News.



While Trump’s comments were brief and did not constitute a formal shift in foreign policy, they added to the debate in Britain over a potential conflict with Argentina, as its leader is becoming increasingly assertive about the territorial claim. Related Article FIFA World Cup ‘Build up the Royal Navy’: UK brawls over Falklands war after World Cup loss to Argentina Argentine President Javier Milei, one of Trump’s ideological allies and the beneficiary of generous White House support, this week declared the islands were a “sacred” claim for his country. Hours after Trump spoke, news emerged from Argentina suggesting Milei wanted to impose sanctions on British oil companies seeking to develop resources near the islands. The move could provoke Britain over the sovereignty of the waters, even though the Sea Lion field is not due to produce any oil until 2028.



Trump has helped Milei before. The White House approved a $US20 billion currency swap with Argentina last year to help stabilise the peso. That contrasted with Trump’s regular complaints about European allies such as the UK. Now there is speculation that Trump will support Milei in laying claim to oil fields around the Falklands because the US could get a share of the action. When GB News asked Trump if he would back Britain in any dispute, the US president praised the UK for winning the 1982 war but cast doubt on whether he would help in another conflict. British paratroopers march across East Falkland island during the 1982 war. Hulton Archive “I was there when they had the first war, that was a long time ago, and I watched it so carefully,” he said.



“And you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly. Related Article Middle East at war The US warship that spent too much time at sea finally gets a break “But it’s a long way away. That’s a big trip. It’s a long way. “So, your country’s not doing well. Don’t forget you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me. Your country was not there to help me.” Trump made the complaint while also repeating his previous claim that the US did not need help from Britain in the war with Iran. He said he asked Starmer if the UK could send a “couple of ships” and was told the UK had none to spare.



The formal US policy on the conflict is to remain neutral on the rival claims. Under the Monroe Doctrine, declared two centuries ago, US administrations see the Americas as their own sphere of influence, not a domain for European powers. Under Trump, the “Donroe Doctrine” dictates that America comes first. And the US president will only help those who give him what he wants – whether it is Greenland or a fleet of ships in the Persian Gulf. While the US said it was neutral in the 1982 war, it leaned toward Britain when Argentina’s military junta ordered an invasion of the islands. US president Ronald Reagan kept up supplies of military material to the UK when British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, sent a fleet to the South Atlantic to reclaim the formal British territory. The British victory was followed by the crumbling of the Argentine military dictatorship, under which an estimated 30,000 people were murdered, and many others were targeted in human rights abuses over eight years.



The Royal Navy had almost 200 vessels at the time of the Falklands War, while it has about 70 today, including some that are being decommissioned. MPs have warned in a series of reports that the country needs a stronger military. Labour MP Tan Dhesi, the chair of the House of Commons defence committee, this week urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to spend more on defence, and he named concerns about the US as one of the reasons. Trump with Argentine President Javier Milei in January, who is seem as one of his major ideological allies. Bloomberg “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority,” Dhesi told parliament. “That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later.”



Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Burnham’s office has issued a statement that repeats the British claim to the Falklands, which have been British territory since 1833 and were first sighted by an English captain in 1592. There were no indigenous inhabitants. The great unknown is how far Milei will go to provoke Britain. He is unpopular at home because his economic vision has failed to generate enough results for the public after decades of hardship. And he faces an election next year, which means he will be desperate enough to resort to patriotic fervour over the islands in the hope it can lift his stocks. Would he start a serious fight? Would he send forces to disrupt oil drilling in contested waters? Would he risk a conflict? That would be utterly irrational.



Even so, the 1982 war has a lesson that still applies today. Some leaders are quite capable of starting stupid wars. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Everyone’s fighting for spots’: This production factory woke a slumbering NRL giant
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Everyone’s fighting for spots’: This production factory woke a slumbering NRL giant Nick Wright September 4, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Kristian Woolf first took the coaching reins at the Dolphins, he was less concerned about what the top squad looked like and more curious about what was under the hood. Before taking the hot seat from inaugural coach Wayne Bennett, he was determined to ensure Redcliffe was a talent factory that would inspire sustainable success – much like the all-conquering Penrith Panthers. That idea dictated his early conversations with Dolphins CEO Terry Reader and Bennett. Once he heard of the involvement of Kurt Richards – who spent 13 years with the Brisbane Broncos and led the Queensland Maroons under-16s, 18s and 19s – Woolf was confident to sign on. Kristian Woolf was eager for a strong development pathway to be put in place ahead of recruitment. NRL Photos “It’s definitely something I was interested in. One of my first conversations with Terry and Wayne was about what we were doing with our academies and who was in charge of that,” Woolf said.



“When I knew that Kurt Richards was in charge of it, I knew we were in good hands, and it was a big part of me wanting to come to the club. When you’ve got those things right, and you’ve got the right people there, you tend to be able to build things for the future.” Related Article Updated

State of Origin ‘I needed to make a change’: The fall and rise of Boyd to Maroons’ top job In the early days, Reader foresaw the side’s fourth season would be the one where the fruits of their academy began to ripen. He was right. Winger Tevita Naufahu and versatile edge forward Brian Pouniu – whose first chance in the back row yielded 179 running metres and 39 tackles against the Eels – have become the maiden graduates of the academy, with lock Lewis Symonds and hooker John Fineanganofo also earning debuts.



Naufahu and Pouniu will take on the Gold Coast Titans on Friday night, with Selwyn Cobbo and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki rested to nurse niggling injuries. “We were obviously really impressed with how he played last time, and what I liked about his performance was he got better as the game went on. He got more and more confident and realised he’s right up to that level,” Woolf said of Pouniu, adding Naufahu had been “one of our best players every time he’s played for us”. A plethora of talent is yet to be tapped into at the top level. Those future hopefuls include two sons of former NRL stars – Noah Fien, whose father Nathan is an assistant at the Dolphins, and Adaquix Luke, whose dad Issac became a South Sydney legend – as well as preseason trial finds Zac Garton (back row) and LJ Nonu (wing). In last year’s maiden NRLQ under-21s series the Dolphins were undefeated, before finishing second in the expanded 12-round competition in 2026, when they finished top of the table, before losing the grand final to the Cowboys 24-22.



“We’ve got a good patch of young blokes coming through, and they challenge us all the time,” Dolphins lock Kurt Donoghoe said. “I think that’s definitely helping out a lot, it makes our training sessions better and the older boys try a little harder. “Everyone’s fighting for spots, everyone’s fighting for each other’s positions. Brian had his debut earlier in the year, and in his second game you could just tell how much better he was for that. Loading “They’ve got so much potential and are really comfortable they can jump in and do a job when we need them.”



Across the club’s opening three seasons, depth had ultimately proven the Dophins’ greatest obstacle. Despite entering the mid-point of the campaigns entrenched in the top eight, they quickly faded as injuries and suspensions cruelled their cause. There has been no such issue in their top-four 2026 finish, with Naufahu starring in the absence of Cobbo, and Pouniu’s breakout performance coming as Connelly Lemuelu fought back from a hamstring issue. Related Article Exclusive

A-League Women Meet the youngest coach in Australian history on a quest to be ‘best ever’ “I think it does make a difference,” Woolf said. “I look at our squad, and Max Plath plays 50 games this week, a couple of weeks ago it was Jack Bostock, a couple of weeks before that it was Kurt Donoghoe. We’ve got a nucleus of guys there who all debuted at this club. “They’ve all become first-graders at this club, some of those have gone on and played representative footy, they all love playing together – you can see when they’re on the field, there’s a real care factor for each other.



“That’s what we want the club to be about. We put a lot of time and effort and finances into our academy to make sure it’s strong and to make sure we’ve got good young players coming through who are well-developed, well-coached, and know what it means to be a Dolphins player.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
