World.title: Auckland business confidence rebounds sharply, latest survey shows
World.content:
Auckland's businesses are feeling much more positive about the region's outlook with a sharp rebound in confidence over the past three months.

The latest Auckland Business Chambers Business Confidence Survey indicates confidence had recovered over the past three months, from the low levels seen during the early days of the Iran war and increase in fuel prices.

Still, the single biggest concern for 64 percent of respondents was consumer confidence, followed by inflation and interest rate anxiety, which had eased back to 46 percent from 55 percent.

Geopolitical and trade risk, which surged to 45 percent in May, had fallen back to 34 percent as the Iran conflict has receded from front-of-mind.

Chamber chief executive Simon Bridges said the negative or very negative reading had dropped to 40 percent in the three months to August, from 54 percent in the period ended May.

"May was as much about what was happening on the other side of the world as it was about anything here at home. The strikes on Iran hit energy costs, inflation expectations and geopolitical risk all at once, and confidence took a real hit. Now, we're seeing a genuine and encouraging bounce back."

Positive sentiment climbed to 26 percent from 15 percent in the three month period. The proportion expecting the economy to decline over the next 12 months was also well up to 24 percent from 10 percent.

Investment and hiring intentions also strengthened.

Plans to invest in the next 12 months rose to 59 percent, from 50 percent, with plans to hire rising 14 points to 50 percent from 36 percent.

Just 8 percent of businesses expected to reduce headcount.

"This isn't just relief. It's businesses regaining the confidence to invest and hire again. That's a real swing in three months," Bridges said.

"The improvement isn't confined to sentiment."

He said the share of businesses reporting performance below expectations fell to 37 percent from 45 percent, with 38 percent seeing year on year revenue growth compared with 37 percent in May.

More than half of businesses were expected to see revenue growth over the next 12 months compared with 43 percent in May.

Businesses were also seeing some improvement on energy costs, with the number finding it unaffordable dropping to 48 percent from 55 percent.

However, unaffordability was still a concern with 81 percent expecting energy costs to keep rising.

Cashflow pressures had also improved with more customers paying on time, with late customer payments dropping to 29 percent from 48 percent in May, which was the most significant improvement in the survey.

Bridges said there was a fast growing concern about AI adoption and digital transformation, which rose to 18 percent from 13 percent in three months.

World.title: Hospitality suffers as spending falls sharply in August
World.content:
Spending growth slowed in August, but travel, recreation and movie theatres remained bright spots as consumers pulled back on hospitality and household goods.

Spending on ANZ cards slowed sharply in August, but New Zealanders still appeared willing to spend on travel and entertainment while remaining cautious elsewhere.

Card spending was flat in August on a seasonally adjusted basis, with annual growth easing to 4.1 percent from 6.1 percent in July.

ANZ noted August was "seldom joyful weather-wise" and said poor weather might have affected spending patterns.

Most major spending categories slipped slightly during the month, but tourism and recreation and non-retail trades and goods both recorded gains.

Spending on airlines and at airports was up 9.4 percent from a year ago. Unsplash

Tourism and recreation spending rose 2.3 percent in August and was 8.8 percent higher than a year earlier.

Spending on airlines and at airports was up 9.4 percent from a year ago, continuing the recovery in travel activity.

Movie theatres were another bright spot. Spending jumped more than 10 percent during the month and was 77.4 percent higher than a year ago.

Whether that's an "Odyssey effect" or just a renewed enthusiasm for the big screen is open to debate, but cinemas are clearly having a moment.

By contrast, spending was softer in some discretionary categories.

Hospitality spending fell 1.0 percent in August after strengthening in July, while housing-related durables dropped 1.3 percent, with every store type in that category recording a monthly decline.

Together, those two categories account for nearly a third of all card spending.

Fuel spending fell 1.5 percent in August despite higher prices at the pump, although it remained 8 percent above year-ago levels.

ANZ said overall spending trends remained mixed, with fuel spending elevated and travel activity continuing to recover.

World.title: Man accused of violent rampage in Auckland's Epsom named as Shalty Heta
World.content:
The man accused of carrying out a violent rampage in the Auckland suburb of Epsom last month can now be named.

He is 49-year-old Shalty Heta.

Heta remains in custody after allegedly assaulting a jogger, taking a car and running down three high-school-aged cyclists, and killing a dog.

Appearing at the Auckland District Court on Friday, he entered a not guilty plea through his lawyer, Jane-Frances O'Halloran.

Judge Evangelos Thomas. Stuff/Ricky Wilson

He did not seek continued name suppression.

Judge Evangelos Thomas set his hearing date for December.

He faced 17 charges including intent to cause grievous bodily harm, which has a maximum penalty of 14 years imprisonment

What police said happened on the day

Police said they were called to reports of a serious assault at the intersection of Ranfurly Rd and Manukau Rd about 7am on August 5.

What followed were described by Auckland City District Commander Superintendent Sunny Patel as six separate incidents.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton said a man without warning had assaulted a woman, causing bruising to her face, head and upper body.

"A member of the public stopped to assist the victim, before this offender has stolen the good Samaritan's vehicle," he said.

Patel confirmed the woman was jogging when she was assaulted by the man who was not wearing any pants, and three our four members of the public came to help her.

"The offender then fled in the stolen vehicle, hitting several vehicles before striking three cyclists who were riding on Manukau Road."

Three students were struck on Manukau Rd. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

After crashing the vehicle, the offender approached a woman walking her dogs.

"The offender has subjected one of the dogs to a violent assault, and sadly the dog has died at the scene," acting Detective Inspector Bolton said.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Patel said police attempted to taser the man once and then were able to taser him and pull him off the dog which had been killed.

"It is a random event that has occurred," he said.

"This has all taken place in full view of the public going about their morning commute."

Police remove bicycles from the scene of a violent incident in the Auckland suburb of Epsom. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Later that day, Patel confirmed the dog had been strangled.

World.title: Australia marks Flag Day by flying New Zealand's flag
World.content:
It's not uncommon to see the New Zealand and Australian flags mixed up at events in other countries, but it seems Aussies can have trouble telling them apart too.

At an event to celebrate 125 years since the Australian flag was first flown, 44 of them were meant to be flown over Capital Hill in Canberra.

But, as 7 News reported, only 42 went up - the other two were the near-identical - but a little bit different - New Zealand flag.

The blunder was spotted and the two rogue flags replaced quickly.

The current Australian flag was first flown above the dome of the Royal Exhibition Building in Melbourne on 3 September 1901, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet said in a statement. Ever since, 3 September has been known as Flag Day.

Its design was chosen from more than 32,000 entries, beating one showing animals playing cricket with a winged ball and another with a kangaroo pointing a gun at the Southern Cross.

It did not become the official flag until 1954.

New Zealand adopted its design, also featuring the Union Jack and some stars, in 1902. A referendum a decade ago on whether to replace it also attracted some unique suggestions, most notably the 'Laser Kiwi', which has become a popular alternative at sports events.

World.title: Union calls for GP practice revamp: 'Let's try a different model'
World.content:
Two medical unions are calling for Health New Zealand to immediately begin employing specialist general practitioners to increase access in underserved areas.

They want public health GPs to work alongside resident doctors training to become GPs.

In a new report, the Resident Doctors Association and the Apex Union also ask Health New Zealand to create a new primary care arm.

The research looks at issues such as growing corporate ownership and the shortage of GPs along with other primary care professionals.

Resident Doctors' Association national secretary Deborah Powell told Nine to Noon there was a problem with retaining GPs plus a "retirement bulge" of GPs was looming.

Call to directly employ GPs for under-served areas Nine To Noon Download MP3 17m

The number of GP trainees had been increased this year which was pleasing, but she stressed there was all manner of models with a rise in corporate ownership of general practices.

Corporates were also involved in the urgent care field so "it's a bit of a mismatch out there".

The union carried out the research to help with providing more employment options for doctors as well as concern over the knock-on effects for emergency departments when patients couldn't access timely primary care.

As well, it was worried that people in high deprivation areas such as Gisborne, Tai Rāwhiti, Northland and Counties Manukau were missing out on services.

About 320,000 people were not enrolled in primary care and many of them were in the deprived areas, Powell said.

"We're saying let's try a different model ....we need to try something different."

She said the paper made a good case for trying its suggested model of a new primary care arm in the deprived areas first.

Under the model, Health NZ would set up the practice and employ the GPs.

Among the staff would be house officers who were already on a pathway towards becoming GPs, registrars and fully qualified GPs.

Physiotherapists, pharmacists, nurses, social workers and psychologists would all have a critical role to play also, Powell said.

The organisation representing GPs, the General Practice Owners Association this week has stressed the importance of GPs, the need for continuity of care and not so much emphasis on TeleHealth.

Powell said GenPro had made a solid case. She was concerned continuity of care was already breaking down, especially in the corporate sector.

Changes the union was advocating would see as one example TeleHealth be integrated into the general practice.

"So when you requested a TeleHealth appointment we would do the best to make sure you saw your regular doctor.

"So we're not looking to move away from best practice in primary care. We're looking to use the technologies we now have to strengthen it."

The community practices the union was advocating would be open beyond regular hours, especially in areas like Manukau.

Community practices would operate for much longer hours than traditional medical centres, Deborah Powell says. 123rf

Corporate ownership trend disturbs union

Powell said general practices have traditionally been owned by GPs and the union was worried about the growing trend for corporates to buy them.

One in four GPs is now employed by a corporate which raised questions of where was the priority for spending.

Corporates had responsibilities to shareholders "so it does shift where money is going to be directed".

Billions of dollars were spent on primary care. GP-run practices prioritised patient care while a corporate must include a focus on delivering a return on investment for shareholders, Powell said.

"So the question inevitably must be asked, is this the best use of public money and where will the priorities sit when it comes to making a decision on spending money to do more for our patients or to satisfy our shareholders."

She added: "Corporatisation is increasing in primary care and I think all New Zealanders should be watching that and asking some questions."

Funding given to primary health organisations (PHOs) for their administration would be better directed going from Health New Zealand directly to community general practices, Powell said.

She said the vaccination programme was one example of where two different organisations (Health NZ and the PHOs) were doubling up.

World.title: Fijian Drua sign former Wallaby forward Isi Naisarani
World.content:
Fiji-born ex-Wallaby forward Isi Naisarani has joined the Fijian Drua ahead of the 2027 Super Rugby Pacific season.

The Fiji-based franchise said Naisarani's singing marked a "significant homecoming" for the No. 8, who left the island a young player to chase an opportunity abroad.

Naisarani has represented the Western Force, ACT Brumbies and Melbourne Rebels during an impressive career in Australia before also taking his talents to Japan.

The club said returning home to play in front of his family and friends, the powerful backrower would bring a wealth of Super Rugby and international experience to the Drua.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Fijian Drua team for the 2027 season. My family and I can't wait to meet and connect with all the fans. Let's make 2027 a good one. Toso Drua Toso!," he said.

Fijian Drua Head coach Brad Mooar said Naisarani joining the Drua family was "very exciting signing for us".

"A dynamic powerful & skilful player he will add a huge amount to our game in attack & in defence. Watching his games in the Shute Shield this year and speaking with Isi it is clear that he is in a great space and is loving his rugby and life," he said.

"Isi is happy, fulfilled and hungry to keep getting better and to give to the Drua - that is a powerful combination! Isi will be outstanding for us"

World.title: Party drug MDMA gets official approval as PTSD treatment
World.content:
Two New Zealand psychiatrists have been approved by MedSafe to prescribe and administer MDMA for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder.

MDMA is a synthetic psychoactive drug used recreationally, often called 'ecstasy', 'E' or 'molly'.

It is the first time Medsafe has granted approvals for this type of therapy.

Until now, MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD has not been available as a treatment option in New Zealand. Australia became the first country to allow authorised psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for PTSD in July 2023.

The two psychiatrists with approval are Wellington's Dr Gary Wynn and Auckland's Dr Tom Paterson. The pair spent more than a year working through the regulatory process, they said in a statement.

Wynn specialises in PTSD and trauma, and Paterson in addiction.

Each round of treatment was expected to cost about $15,000. A standard course would be three rounds, totalling 54 hours of therapy.

No public funding has yet been allocated.

Associate Health Minister David Seymour said MDMA "can be very effective at treating [PTSD] through psychedelic-assisted therapy".

"Recent changes have put New Zealand's settings in line with Australia, where authorised prescribers have been providing MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD in clinical settings for some time.

"MDMA remains an unapproved medicine, but two experienced psychiatrists have already been granted authority to prescribe it to patients with PTSD.

"This is very good news for their patients, who will have been suffering for some time."

He said there would be safeguards in place to ensure it was prescribed safely.

"Treatment with MDMA occurs as part of a comprehensive treatment plan and occurs in the prescriber's clinic. Patients don't get dispensed MDMA to take home.

"Practitioners must also meet a series of requirements to gain approval, including demonstrating expertise in the area and providing a detailed proposal of how they will administer the treatment."

World.title: 'Manufestos and wings': The new twist in this month's Bird of the Year competition
World.content:
Voting for Forest & Bird's Bird of the Year opens Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The country's politicians aren't the only ones gearing up for an election as Forest & Bird's 2026 Bird of the Year opens for voting.

Voting kicked off on Friday and will close on September 20, Forest & Bird's acting chief executive Erika Toleman, told Morning Report.

But this year, the avian election comes with a twist - Aotearoa's manu have been sorted into six different political parties - the shore birds, the floor birds, the tree birds, the sea birds, the high birds and the shy birds.

Each vote cast for a bird will also count towards its party's total, so there would be not only a bird of the year but a favourite flock.

"They're not arranged along traditional human political lines in our election," Toleman said. "Every candidate has a left wing and a right wing and each party has a manufesto.

"Like with any election there could be scandal along the way, we expect some ruffled feathers around the house."

Toleman made it clear no bats were in the running this year, despite the long-tailed bat winning against the other feathered frontrunners in 2021.

Toleman said one of her favourite birds in the running this year that may be a more unlikely favourite was the Western Petrel, Tāiko.

"It's this gigantic bird, our largest burrowing petrel on the mainland which breeds in one place in the world... like many young New Zealanders it does it's OE and goes over to Chile and when it's ready it comes back and has its babies here."

The youth vote would be important in the voting this year, Toleman said, with up to 400 schools registered to participate and tamariki votes would act as special votes.

"Unlike the other election this year, the kids are actually gonna have the ability to swing this election right at the last minute. So you'll have to wait to the last minute to see what takes the perch."

While Bird of the Year was a bit of fun, Toleman said it was also a way to shine the spotlight on the fact our native birds were in some trouble.

She said it was about celebrating and explaining to people about what help was needed.

Every voter could cast five votes on the Bird of the Year website where more information could be found about the candidates.

World.title: After his Broncos ending, a new beginning looms for Payne Haas
World.content:
A dead rubber game in an empty stadium was no way for Payne Haas's time as a Bronco to come to an end.

To match what he's produced in nine seasons with Brisbane that averaged out to magnificent, Haas's last game would've needed to feel like a life and death struggle where the winners touched the heavens and defeat sent the fallen screaming into hell.

Such contests have been where Haas has enjoyed some of his finest hours and those are the games of 159 appearances for Brisbane that have made him a living legend.

NRL live The Broncos win a final-round contest against the Bulldogs, in a game that doubled as Payne Haas's farewell from Brisbane. Follow live.

But for the last before he heads to South Sydney, he had to settle for purgatory.

Brisbane's 34-20 win against Canterbury on Thursday night felt like so many other games that happen as non-finals teams grimly march to the end of the season.

Tackles were made, tries were scored and whistles were blown on a night that felt flat and lonely, as the citadel of Stadium Australia often can be with nearly 70,000 empty seats.

Brisbane did send Haas out a winner, and that still matters. Josiah Karapani played a blinder and the Broncos found a little of the football that marked that championship season last year.

Haas got in the action early, smashing his way through four defenders to score the opening try of the night and later spent time in the sin bin after being pinged for repeated infringements.

With 152 metres across 71 minutes the numbers were strong, as they always are for Haas, but it's important not to get lost in them.

While the match as a spectacle and a contest was not a fitting finale for Haas's Brisbane career as a whole, it made much more sense as the close for what has been an uneven year in comparison to his other campaigns.

Haas has not played poorly and even if he had, a poor Payne Haas game would be a stand-out performance for many other props.

You could say he's good enough on a bad day but he hasn't had enough truly bad days for us to be sure.

Haas has still averaged 156 run metres and just under 35 tackles a game, marks many players would be proud to call their own.

In 2026, Payne Haas has not quite hit the superhuman form he's become known for. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

He has still had big moments, like his rampaging try against the Bulldogs on his last night, or his similar effort against Canberra two weeks ago that kicked off a rollicking Broncos comeback win.

Australia and Samoa would still both crawl over broken glass to have him in their World Cup sides because he is still the best prop on the planet.

But Haas has not quite been superhuman, and that is what we have become accustomed to during his Bronco years.

We are used to him being closer to a miracle than a man — 156 metres per game, somehow, is the second-lowest average of his career as a starter.

His offloads have plummeted, from 70 last year to just 21 this season. So too his tackle busts, which have fallen from 130 to 64 with the wide-running charges that became such a feature of his game in recent years seemingly hard to find.

In similarly short supply are the inexplicable, gut-busting efforts to cover the defensive mistake of a teammate or clean up a loose ball or just generally be where no prop forward ever should be to do a little extra that no other prop forward can ever really do.

After making the Dally M team of the year four of the past five seasons, Payne Haas will miss out in 2026. (AAP: Jono Searle)

After making the Dally M team of the year four times in the past five seasons — with a 14-match year in 2024 marking his only exclusion — Haas will miss out this year and rightly so.

The Roosters' blunt-force artist Naufahu Whyte and New Zealand's James Fisher-Harris have both enjoyed better seasons.

So too has the old iron Cowboy himself, Jason Taumalolo, and the greatest forward of an age now past got the better of Haas in both of North Queensland's wins over their southern rivals.

Mitch Barnett, Haas's replacement in Brisbane for next year, did the same last month when the Warriors beat the Broncos up like they owed them money.

Even players outside the top eight have got a bit of a turn to put one on the living legend.

Haas barely ever misses tackles — he made 40 without a single miss against Canterbury — but last week against Melbourne Stefano Utoikamanu brushed past him for a try the Storm man can tell the grandkids about because it's not every day you get one on the king.

Haas is not the only player at Brisbane who has struggled to deal with the premiership hangover but he is the only player who seemed above such things. Motivation is fleeting, it comes and it goes and that is why it's for humans, not heroes.

Haas is the player who goes all day, every day, no matter what and he has done it on worse Bronco teams than this.

In the final game of the 2020 season, when Brisbane lost to North Queensland to confirm their first wooden spoon on as low a night as the club has ever had, it was a breakaway try to Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow that confirmed the result.

Chasing Tabuai-Fidow, then or now, is to put in maximum effort for a futile cause at the best of times, let alone in the dying stages of the final game of a nightmare season.

But there going after him, as sure as the sun will rise tomorrow, was Payne Haas. It didn't make a difference, but Haas did it just in case it might.

Last year's premiership was Payne Haas's ultimate reward. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

He kept going like that until it felt like a way of life, until years later when he lifted the premiership trophy and confirmed a legacy that meant he could stand alongside the likes of Glenn Lazarus, Shane Webcke and Petero Civoniceva as the greatest forwards in Brisbane's history.

That journey to greatness is in starker relief given his first Brisbane years began in low-down valleys, making the trail he forged all the way to a premiership his Everest.

His sense of triumph and relief was palpable after that grand final win even amid the throng of family, friends and backslappers that filled the Brisbane sheds as the air felt thick with emotion and cigar smoke.

The player who always found more to do at last had some satisfaction. The seemingly endless appetite for the grind and the fight was satiated.

It was the culmination of Haas's entire footballing life and if anyone had earned the right to look a little more mortal in the aftermath, it was him.

Why Haas's move changes the fate of two NRL giants Payne Haas's decision to leave Brisbane for South Sydney in 2027 didn't just shock the rugby league world, it transformed the futures of two of rugby league's most powerful clubs in an instant.

This version of Payne Haas is still more than good enough to impact the premiership race. If this is the new normal he will still be mighty for South Sydney in a way few players can ever dream of and regardless of what happens next, his greatness is already assured.

But there's every chance the move now creates the chance for another rise, in a new city with new colours and a fresh start amid new challenge that will, from time to time, demand he again pushes himself beyond reasonable limits.

As hyperbolic as we can get about players of Haas's ilk, they are still human. They still need something to chase and last year, after so much effort and so much time, Haas made his ultimate catch.

Perhaps it meant that his farewell season as a Bronco, and particularly his final night, could not match what has come before.

But even if it wasn't a fitting end to what was, it is still an end — which means a new beginning can follow.

World.title: So good for so long this year, Dockers wilt at inopportune time against Hawks
World.content:
So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — its worst shift of the AFL season.

But that assessment is unkind to a Hawthorn side who were nothing short of brilliant in Thursday night's qualifying final at Perth Stadium.

The Hawks dominated on the ground, in the air and particularly down back, holding Fremantle to 40 points, its lowest score of the season.

The victory was built on manic pressure, the visitors forcing the Dockers into turnovers and denying them the chance to get their running game going.

Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth Hawthorn will host an MCG preliminary final after an upset 32-point win over minor premier Fremantle in Perth.

Hawthorn's 32-point win puts it into a home preliminary final, the club now two MCG wins away from its 14th premiership.

Fremantle, meanwhile, toppled from joint-premiership favouritism, and will have to do it the hard way if the club is to bring a first flag to the port city.

The concerning thing for the Dockers was the manner of the defeat.

No Wharfie Time

Other than the first two minutes of the game, the result rarely looked in doubt.

There would be no Wharfie Time comeback against the Hawks this time, as there had been in round nine when the Dockers emerged from a titanic scrap with a 15-point win.

The Hawks came, saw and conquered the Dockers at Perth Stadium. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

Last night Fremantle, who had been unbeaten at home all year, just couldn't get close enough to push the button.

So good was Hawthorn's defence that the Dockers' three-headed forward line leviathan — Josh Treacy, Jye Amiss and Pat Voss — combined for only two goals.

Voss and Treacy managed just one mark between them.

Credit must go to Hawthorn's three-headed beast of its own — backmen James Sicily, Josh Battle and Tom Barrass proving majestic in getting their blend of destruction and creativity just right.

James Sicily was masterful in defence for the Hawks. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

After Fremantle kicked the opening goal of the match, Hawthorn then banged on the next six to take a 33-point lead into the long break.

The Dockers needed to make a move in the third quarter, and they emerged from the sheds with renewed vigour.

But every time Freo struck, the Hawks replied.

The Dockers failed to kick two goals in a row all night, and most of the 59,446 fans who poured through the turnstiles would have been resigned to their fate long before the final siren.

On a night when few Dockers beat their direct opponents, Jordan Clark was outstanding — the All Australian defender notching up 38 disposals and dragging down a spectacular mark.

Sicily was Hawthorn's best with 26 touches, while Jack Gunston, Dylan Moore and Nick Watson kicked two goals apiece.

'Not dead and buried'

Speaking after the match, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir backed his decision to select Brandon Walker for his first game since round one to curtail the influence of Nick Watson, describing their contest as a "pretty good tussle".

But Walker's rolled ankle ended that tussle early, the dashing defender in tears on the bench after being ruled out of the game.

Watson capitalised on his absence, kicking a goal late in the third quarter and then producing a moment of pure wizardry early in the fourth, handballing to himself before burning off Luke Ryan to set up a goal for Harry Morrison, who extended the lead to 38 points.

Nick Watson prepares to activate the jets to get past Luke Ryan and send Hawthorn inside 50. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

There was no way back for the Dockers, who have now lost three of their past four games.

But Longmuir denied his side was out of form.

"Go back and have a look at the Adelaide game [in round 23], I thought we played a good brand of footy against a really desperate team who had it all to play for," he said.

"We had a couple of away games where we didn't play our best footy, but I've got a lot of faith in this group to bounce back from that."

The coach, who has preached the value of "process" all year, backed his men to get the process spot on over the next week ahead of a cut-throat home semi-final against either Carlton or Geelong.

"It's not the way we wanted it to go, but we're not dead and buried," he said.

Emotional win

For Hawks coach Sam Mitchell, the overwhelming feeling was one of pride.

Teams like Geelong, Sydney and Adelaide had been able to meet Fremantle's fire for quarters and halves this season, but no one has been able to douse it completely for an entire game at Perth Stadium like the Hawks.

Sam Mitchell was proud of the intensity his players showed. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"The relentless pressure that we had on them in that game was what we thought would be required," Mitchell said.

" Full credit to the players for being able to produce that level of effort for that long. "

The coach paid tribute to Will Day, the midfielder outstanding in his first final after a dreadful run with injuries.

An emotional Day let the tears flow on the final siren, and Mitchell said he was feeling it too.

"He's so resilient, he's been through so much," Mitchell said.

"He showed it more than I did, but I felt exactly the way he looked after the game."

World.title: Kiss makes selection gamble for Wallabies-Argentina rematch
World.content:
Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been thrust back into the Wallabies' starting side while Ben Donaldson will steer the ship in Mendoza for his first start at fly-half in two years.

After a tight win a week earlier, coach Les Kiss has again tinkered with his side for their Argentina rematch on Sunday morning (AEST).

After a run of six losses, the side is chasing five-straight wins for the first time since 2021.

Carter Gordon, reportedly under an injury cloud during the week, has been shifted to the bench to give perennial back-up Donaldson a rare start in the number 10 jersey.

Ryan Lonergan will remain at scrum half, and Tom Wright will play his 50th Test after being named at fullback.

Billy Pollard and Josh Nasser will share the hooking duties, with Brandon Paenga-Amosa rotated out.

It's otherwise a full-strength pack with Angus Bell, Taniela Tupou, Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams all starting, while Harry Wilson has been recalled at number 8 alongside Fraser McReight and Rob Valetini.

Kiss has switched his centres though, with Isaac Henry benched and Hunter Paisami left out to make room for star pair Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii will line up at centre. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

It will be the first time that pair, who were midfield regulars under Joe Schmidt, start together under Kiss, who is 3-0 as Test coach.

Fililipo Daugunu will earn his first start of the season on the wing, replacing Harry Potter, while Kalani Thomas takes Reds teammate Tate McDermott's spot on the bench as back-up scrum-half.

Prop Aidan Ross and lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto also come into the side on the bench, with Charlie Cale the back row back-up.

Meanwhile, Argentina coach Felipe Contepomi has made a number of changes as they look to square the series.

Locks Efraín Elías and Franco Molina come in to replace Tomás Lavanini and Guido Petti, who shifts to the flank in place of Benjamín Grondona.

Pedro Delgado comes in at tighthead prop in place of Francisco Moreno, who drops to the bench in the last of the four changes in the pack.

In the backs, the inexperienced 26-year-old Benetton 10 Nicolás Roger comes into the side at fly-half, outside Newcastle scrum-half Simón Benítez Cruz, while Bath 15 Santiago Carreras switches to fullback to replace Gerónimo Prisciantelli.

Two uncapped players — Facundo Cardozo and Mateo Soler — are in line to make their international debuts off the bench after being named among the replacements.

Pablo Matera, winning his 126th cap, continues as captain in the absence of Julián Montoya, who is one of several overseas-based players unavailable for selection, having not been released by his French side, Section Paloise Béarn Pyrénées.

Wallabies team to face Argentina: Angus Bell, Billy Pollard, Taniela Tupou; Josh Canham, Jeremy Williams; Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson; Ryan Lonergan, Ben Donaldson; Filipo Daugunu, Len Ikitau, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen; Tom Wright. Bench: Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Kalani Thomas, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry.

AAP/Reuters

World.title: Osaka, Keys overcome mid-match stumbles to fight on at US Open
World.content:
Two-time champion Naomi Osaka overcame mid-match mistakes to progress while Madison Keys saved five match points to keep her campaign alive in the US Open second round, as fans eagerly awaited Coco Gauff and Alexander Zverev in the late program.

A perennial fan favourite in New York, Osaka survived an up-and-down affair against Czech Kateřina Siniaková to win 6-2 5-7 6-1, harnessing the mental resolve she has taken years to hone on the court where she claimed her maiden major eight years ago.

Sweeny soars into US Open last 32 Australian wildcard Dane Sweeny has posted the biggest win of his career, upsetting dual grand slam semifinalist Lorenzo Musetti to make the US Open's last 32.

"I just told myself that it's an honour to play on this court," Osaka told the crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I just want to keep playing in front of you guys if possible."

The 28-year-old Japanese player's match was not the only nail-biter across the sprawling Flushing Meadows plaza, as American Keys mounted an epic comeback against Hungarian Anna Bondár to win 5-7 6-4 7-6 (5) to delight the home fans on the outer courts.

The 2017 finalist sent over a remarkable 34 forehand winners to get the job done and gave all credit to her adoring fans after forcing Bondár into an error at the net on match point.

Madison Keys saved five match points in her three-set epic. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

"That was something, huh?" Keys, 31, told the crowd after the win.

"No stress though — we all knew I had it, right?"

Her compatriot Taylor Fritz had a far easier time, swatting aside Italian Mattia Bellucci 6-0 6-1 6-1, while Amanda Anisimova's 6-3 3-6 6-1 defeat of Austrian Lilli Tagger added to the American joy.

Canadian third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime, a semi-finalist last year, took the first set but was then swept away in a 6-7(5) 6-3 6-2 6-2 defeat by Russian Karen Khachanov, becoming the highest-seeded man to exit the tournament so far.

The Philippines' wildly popular Alex Eala capped the early programme at Louis Armstrong Stadium with a comprehensive 6-1 6-4 defeat of Ukraine's Oleksandra Oliynykova.

Days of stubborn rain gave way to sunny skies in New York, where Iga Świątek enjoyed a relatively drama-free 6-3 6-2 win over Argentina's Nadia Podoroska, in a rare appearance on the outdoor courts for the 2022 champion.

Fans will eagerly await another evening programme packed with talent as fourth-seeded 2023 champion Gauff kicks off the night on Ashe against Paula Badosa, followed by the men's top seed Zverev, who plays France's Quentin Halys.

Frenchman Gaël Monfils will hope to make magic again in his farewell season when he faces 14th-seeded American Learner Tien in the first night match at Armstrong before second seed Elena Rybakina plays Spain's Jessica Bouzas Maneiro.

Reuters

World.title: FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' over World Cup sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA accused UEFA of waging a "smear campaign" against it and president Gianni Infantino, escalating a dispute over the abandoned proposal to sell a stake in the world governing body's commercial rights, according to a court filing seen by Reuters.

UEFA last week submitted an ex parte application in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York seeking permission to obtain testimony and documents from US-based entities for use in potential criminal proceedings in Switzerland.

"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA's smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.

Reuters has contacted FIFA and UEFA for comment.

UEFA said it was considering criminal proceedings against Infantino and other FIFA officials over FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a proposed entity that would have held commercial rights linked to the men's and women's World Cups.

UEFA alleged the proposal was developed without adequate consultation with FIFA's governing bodies and 211 member associations.

In a motion to intervene seen by Reuters filed on September 1 by FIFA (AMERICAS) Inc. and FWC2026 US, Inc., FIFA asked the court to defer ruling on UEFA's application or allow it to oppose the request.

FIFA argued that UEFA was seeking discovery for "purportedly contemplated (but non-existent) Swiss criminal proceedings". The world governing body also alleged UEFA had sought to derail the FFE proposal from the outset.

The proposal was withdrawn on July 31 after opposition from UEFA and other regional governing bodies.

"Rather than participate in that democratic process, UEFA issued a press release, the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.

FIFA further argued that UEFA's opposition was motivated by a desire to preserve European football's dominance.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

Infantino, up for re-election for a fourth term in March 2027, has been criticised since tabling the now-abandoned proposal, with several countries withdrawing their support for his candidacy.

The Swiss-Italian administrator is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The regional governing bodies have discussed a potential vote of no confidence in Infantino.

Infantino, who retains support from the African and South American confederations, has sought to sideline the confederations and appeal directly to individual members.

UEFA, in a statement last week, said that it would work with partner confederations to ensure member associations are offered a "credible alternative" committed to reform, if Infantino seeks another term.

UEFA also provisionally suspended plans to boycott FIFA competitions, paving the way for all qualified teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland, the first major tournament that could have been affected by the stand-off.

However, the body said its members had unanimously mandated the confederation to pursue "every available institutional, political and legal avenue" to secure reforms and restore limits on presidential authority.

The confederation also called for "a genuinely independent external review" of the failed FIFA proposal, saying: "FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions."

Reuters

World.title: Stars, stakes and heartbreak as Crows, Bulldogs prepare for blockbuster final
World.content:
While the weekly battles between AFL teams on the field are the ones that draw the crowds, the drama and intrigue off the field can be just as compelling.

After an emotional Wildcard weekend; the footy world will fixate on a sold-out Adelaide Oval Saturday night for a high stakes elimination final between Adelaide and the Western Bulldogs; that is packed to the brim with must-watch narratives starting with the Crows senior coach.

Two weeks ago, the ABC flagged the immense pressure facing Matthew Nicks after the club's historic straight sets exit last season; but now that ideology has devolved into a public performance review with reports a loss would see the senior coach's tenure come to a premature end.

Language is important in an industry where "full support of the board" statements are well known for being a death knell for a senior coach, but Adelaide CEO Tim Silvers, president John Olsen and Nicks himself have failed to definitively deny the claim when asked outright if he's coaching for his career.

"He has a year to run on his contract, and we expect him to be coaching our team next year," Olsen said on Tuesday.

"Matthew Nicks has been a great coach for our footy club … he's leading us into his second successive finals campaign," Silvers deflected the next day.

"I understand the narrative, it's part of this industry, but it's probably not something I can talk to … there's always an understanding that performance is needed," Nicks followed.

Matthew Nicks has faced questions about his coaching future with Crows this week. (AAP: Jason O'Brien)

The problem facing Adelaide is the Western Bulldogs are no strangers to handing out a shock finals thumping at Adelaide Oval; toppling Port Adelaide by 71-points in a preliminary final five years ago.

Who has the edge?

Luke Beveridge's side is hoping to come full circle.

Every year the Dogs have won a final under Beveridge they have made it all the way to the end of September and 10 years ago they became the first side to ever win the flag from seventh.

Their season has been littered with injuries and now they must overcome the loss of midfield bull Matthew Kennedy who suffered a concussion against Collingwood.

Four-time Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes the new finals structure will severely disadvantage the wildcard winners due to the physical toll.

"That's one of the negatives of the Wildcard Round, sides that get through are up against it," he said on SA Grandstand.

When the Bulldogs have won finals under Luke Beveridge, they've made it through to that year's decider. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

Hall of Fame Mick Malthouse agreed on AFL Saturday.

"They play straight into the hands of fifth… there's too many games and the players are worn out," he said.

Kennedy's loss is a big blow given clearance dominance is a key part of the Dogs offence; with their 33 points from centre bounce last Friday the most the club has ever scored in a final.

It's an anxiety inducing stat for Adelaide who were the worst side in the final month of 2025 for clearance differential and lost first possession by a massive 31 in the semi-final against Hawthorn.

The difference for the Crows in 2026 might just be the man who missed finals footy last year through suspension Izak Rankine, who is in the midst of the fourth best seven-game run on record; averaging 156 rating points mirroring Chris Judd in 2006 and only two points behind the best-ever in Patrick Dangerfield in 2017.

Rankine's journey to his first finals campaign comes after a tumultuous end to the 2025 season, where he was banned for four games after making a homophobic slur.

Izak Rankine has been a game changer for the Crows in the latter stages of this season. (AAP: Matt Turner)

He told ABC Sport back in July that he feels he can be the missing piece.

"Sitting out last year and watching the boys not get the job done created a real hunger in my belly," he said.

"I want to make sure I'm helping the team out as much as I can … we want to prove a lot of people wrong."

True heavyweight clash

In the last 10 weeks, the Crows are third for score from centre bounce differential and clearances, the Dogs are fourth in both stats.

It's a match-up that will get main-event billing in any round, let alone a sudden death showdown with Jordan Dawson, Rankine, Bontempelli and Richards combining for 12 All-Australian blazers; but the headline attraction is up forward with Taylor Walker entering his final game at Adelaide Oval.

The 36-year-old is the club and venue's all-time leading goal kicker and is eager for his farewell tour to end with a fairytale flag.

"If we can look each other in the eye at the end of whenever we finish and say that we had a crack and we had a swing at trying to win the premiership, then I'll be fully content with what we've been able to achieve," he said.

Crows fans will be hungry to taste first finals victory since 2017. (AAP: David Mariuz)

After losing in a thriller to the Dogs in Round 2, Crows fans will be hoping this weekend's final plays out more like their Round 14 affair that saw Adelaide win by 57-points.

If it ends up being a nailbiter, picking a winner will be an absolute roulette with Luke Beveridge's men unbeaten in the seven games they've played that featured a margin of a goal or less and have a record of 9-1-1 across the last two seasons.

The Crows meanwhile have had three wins by a point in 2026 and a record of 6-4 since 2024.

It shapes as a true heavyweight clash at the Adelaide Oval Saturday night; packed with narratives, stars, drama, elation and heartbreak. It's top shelf viewing (that's made even better when you sync up the ABC Sport commentary).

You can hear the ABC's call of the elimination final between Adelaide and the Western Bulldogs from 6.30pm CST.

World.title: Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth
World.content:
James Sicily (right) had a huge night in the Hawks' backline as his team took care of the Dockers in the west (Getty Images)

The Hawks kicked six goals to one in a dominant first half in Thursday night's clash to set up the 10.12 (72) to 5.10 (40) win and secure a home preliminary final.

Fremantle, who had been a perfect 12-0 at Perth Stadium this season, will now confront either Carlton or Geelong in a cut-throat semi-final in Perth next week.

The Dockers were a dominant force during the home-and-away season, stringing together a 14-game winning streak at one stage on the way to a league-best 19-4 record.

But the minor premiers looked overawed in the finals cauldron on Thursday night in front of 59,446 fans — Fremantle's largest ever home crowd.

Fremantle's first-half return of 1.4 (10) was their lowest such score in a final, even worse than the 1.6 (12) they kicked across the opening two quarters of their 2013 grand final loss to the Hawks.

The Dockers will now have to win their semi-final and then an away preliminary final in order to make their first grand final since 2013.

Sicily, Tom Barrass and Josh Battle were rocks in defence, keeping Jye Amiss, Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss to two goals and 19 disposals between the three of them.

Treacy's first kick of the game — a set-shot goal — only arrived with five minutes remaining in the match.

Hawks veteran Jack Gunston kicked two clutch goals in the first-half onslaught, while Dylan Moore chipped in with two majors.

Watson was a human highlights reel at times on the way to two goals from 19 disposals.

"The belief in the group's outstanding," Watson told Fox Sports after the match.

"We knew it was going to be hot. It was hot early, but the boys stood up well."

Fremantle ruckman Luke Jackson kicked the opening goal of the match, but the rest of the first half belonged to Hawthorn as their slick ball movement and fierce tackling left the Dockers looking second-rate at times.

Watson's soccered goal from nearly 20m out sparked a run of four consecutive goals as the Hawks took a surprise 28-9 lead into quarter-time.

Hawthorn's pressure continued to be off the charts in the second term.

And even when Fremantle hit back — like when Karl Worner won a holding-the-ball free kick for his chasing tackle on Max Beattie — the Hawks didn't give up.

When Worner played on and took a bounce from that free kick, Beattie ran hard to put pressure on the kick.

It resulted in a turnover and a running goal to Moore as Hawthorn's lead expanded to 33 points by half-time.

There wasn't anything obvious in the half-time stats to suggest what was going wrong for Fremantle.

But the naked eye could decipher their problem — an inability to handle Hawthorn's intense pressure.

Jordan Clark's high-flying mark on top of Jack Ginnivan was a rare highlight for Fremantle in the first half.

Hawthorn forward Mitch Lewis suffered a huge scare when he hurt his shoulder in a heavy landing, but he was able to return for the start of the second half.

Fremantle broke Hawthorn's run of six goals when Jye Amiss kicked truly one minute into the third quarter.

But luck wasn't on Fremantle's side, with Watson kicking his second to restore the 33-point margin at the final change after his direct opponent Brandon Walker had rolled his ankle in the previous play.

Watson put the icing on the cake early in the final quarter when he gathered the ball at full pace on the wing, handballed to himself while under pressure from Luke Ryan, before regathering to kick it to Harry Morrison for the sealing goal.

AAP

World.title: Broncos send Haas out a winner with top score of 2026 against Dogs
World.content:
The Broncos have won a final-round contest against the Bulldogs 34-20, in a game that doubled as superstar prop Payne Haas's farewell from Brisbane.

Haas scored the opening try as the Broncos notched up their equal highest score of a disappointing 2026 season, tied with their tally from a 34-30 win over the Raiders four weeks earlier.

Halfback Ben Hunt said the team had extra motivation to send Haas out a winner before he heads to South Sydney from 2027.

"Payne means a hell of a lot to this club, he really does," Hunt told ABC Sport.

"It's been a very disappointing year, but to come out here tonight, the boys really carried themselves in a great way and really showed up for Payne.

"He deserved the win tonight."

The teams were tied 10-10 at half-time, but the Broncos, sparked by Hunt and hooker Billy Walters, exploded after the break with four tries in 15 minutes to jump out to a 24-point lead.

Canterbury hit back with tries to Viliame Kikau and Lachlan Galvin, but they could not get close enough to truly challenge the Broncos, who will finish 14th or 15th in their failed premiership defence.

Look back all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

Tech.title: You can watch the coolant flow inside Ugreen’s liquid-cooled power bank
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Does your power bank have “CryoPulse technology” or a “Cyber Window”? If you disappointingly answered “no” to both, you might want to consider upgrading to Ugreen’s new MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank. It’s available starting today for $149.99, which puts it on the really expensive end of power banks with only a 10,000mAh battery, but those fancy-sounding features are part of what Ugreen is claiming to be the world’s first liquid-cooling system on a power bank with wireless charging.

Inside the MagFlow Pro is a micro-pump that’s used to circulate coolant and draw heat away from components including the power bank’s Qi2.2-compatible wireless charging coil. You can see the coolant flowing through a (cyber) window on the front of the power bank. That system works alongside copper foil and a design that keeps charging components separated to help reduce heat buildup to prolong the life of the power bank’s battery, the life of your phone, and to help maintain up to 25W of power delivery. It should result in leaving the MagFlow Pro cooler to the touch after a long charging session.

The power bank’s lanyard doubles as a built-in USB-C charging cable, while an additional USB-C port can be used to charge a third device. Image: Ugreen

In addition to charging devices wirelessly, the power bank has a built-in USB-C cable lanyard and a USB-C port that can both charge devices at up to 45W, but that’s also the maximum output of the MagFlow Pro, so connecting multiple devices will reduce charging rates.

Tech.title: Congressman says TikTok backed out of a meeting to avoid child safety questions
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

TikTok backed out of a congressional committee’s “public roundtable” set for this month over concerns it would be asked about child safety practices, the chair of the committee said.

After negotiating “in good faith” to bring TikTok’s chief security officer before the House Select Committee on China to answer questions about Chinese government access to Americans’ data and the TikTok algorithm, Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said in a statement Thursday that the company reversed course. “Now, TikTok is refusing to appear citing its own desire to avoid broader scrutiny of its child safety practices,” Moolenaar wrote. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

TikTok reneged on its commitment on August 27th, Moolenaar told Bloomberg in an interview — a day after Meta reached its sweeping settlement with state attorneys general and called on TikTok and YouTube to follow suit. All three of those tech platforms still have many pending suits focused on their child safety practices. “They claimed that in light of Meta’s settlement with state attorneys general, they wouldn’t be able to answer questions on child-safety issues,” Moolenaar told Bloomberg, even though he said the meeting was not set to focus on that topic.

“They claimed that in light of Meta’s settlement with state attorneys general, they wouldn’t be able to answer questions on child-safety issues”

Moolenaar said in his statement that the committee would attempt to reschedule. “We will continue to work in good faith to protect the American people and ensure TikTok executives publicly address the Committee’s questions regarding its operations and safeguards – consistent with the requirements of the Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act – before the end of the year.”

The law Moolenaar references is the one that briefly banned TikTok from the US, before enforcement was repeatedly delayed by President Donald Trump. Ultimately, a deal to make its US service part of a new entity closed in January, theoretically resolving the security issues the law cited. But lawmakers on the Select Committee had lingering concerns even after that happened. In a statement after the deal closed, Moolenaar said TikTok would need to answer questions about Chinese government influence on the algorithm and US data protection to the committee directly.
